#5730. Safety of Controversial Vasculitis Drug Bolstered in Dedicated Trial

— Findings might help avacopan's fight to stay in the U.S. market

ORLANDO -- Interim results from a prospective trial designed to evaluate safety of avacopan (Tavneos), the embattled drug for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV), indicated that the product could still avoid total extinction.

Patients receiving avacopan in the trial, dubbed AvacoStar, experienced a fourfold higher rate of liver abnormalities compared with those treated instead with rituximab (Rituxan) or cyclophosphamide, as Bernhard Hellmich, MD, of the University of Tübingen in Germany, reported at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting.

However, these liver abnormalities were neither common nor severe, and other significant adverse effects were no more common with avacopan than with the standard-of-care alternatives.

The findings should be a welcome boost for avacopan, for which 2026 was a very bad year. When it was approved for AAV in 2021, this drug that targets the complement pathway was seen as a valuable addition to treatment options. AAV was treated historically with corticosteroids, despite the serious adverse effects that come with chronic use. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide then joined the armamentarium, but they carry safety risks as well.

Avacopan ran into trouble earlier this year when it was revealed that its original developer, ChemoCentryx, had results from the drug's pivotal registration trial "readjudicated" after unblinding, which shifted some patients from nonresponders to responders. The original findings indicated that the primary endpoint was missed; following the changes, it was achieved.

The appearance of data manipulation set off a firestorm. Liver abnormalities were a known issue with avacopan, but a label warning was considered enough to mitigate the risks. But when the readjudication was discovered, the FDA asked Amgen, which assumed control of avacopan in the U.S. after buying ChemoCentryx in 2022, to take the drug off the market voluntarily. The liver problems gained even more prominence in March when the FDA linked avacopan to eight deaths and 76 worldwide cases of drug-induced liver injury, including 54 hospitalizations.

Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, the controversy over data integrity in the pivotal trial prompted British and European regulators to order avacopan's withdrawal. Its marketing authorization was revoked in August in the European Union, while its withdrawal in the U.K. will be completed by this coming March.

Thus far, Amgen has rejected the FDA's withdrawal request, and the agency has not made it mandatory. Findings from the new safety study, along with an Italian study published last month that confirmed avacopan's efficacy in AAV, might be enough to keep the drug available in the U.S., at least for the time being.

AvacoStar was started in 2023 by Vifor Fresenius Medical Care Renal Pharma -- a joint venture between Fresenius Medical Care and what is now CSL Vifor, which had licensed avacopan from ChemoCentryx in Europe and felt a dedicated safety study was needed. The study enrolled 504 patients with highly active AAV in Britain and Germany who would be given either avacopan or one of the more conventional alternatives at clinicians' discretion, with 254 receiving avacopan and 250 an alternative regimen.

Outcomes were four types of "medical events of special interest," which included liver injury, cardiovascular events, serious infections, and malignancies -- altogether with 101 events in 72 patients (28.3%, 0.30 per patient-year). These were identified from participants' subsequent medical records. The study is still ongoing, with final completion scheduled in 2030. Hellmich's report involved data extracted as of September 2025, at which point more than 95% of patients were still on their original therapy, with mean duration of 16.2 months for avacopan and 12.7 months for the alternatives.

Mean patient age was about 64, and half of them were men. Specific AAV subtypes were equally split between granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. Almost three-quarters of patients were newly diagnosed. Half of them had serious renal impairment, including some 20% with estimated glomerular filtration rate less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2.

Liver injury was the only medical event of special interest that was significantly more common with avacopan (IRR 4.03, 95% CI 1.55-10.48), and the absolute rate was reassuringly low, at 0.07 per patient-year (95% CI 0.05-0.10). Serious infections were the most common, at 0.14 per patient-year in the avacopan group, compared with 0.18 per patient-year with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Cardiac events occurred at 0.09 per patient-year in both groups, and malignancies were also seen at equal rates, 0.02 per patient-year.

Most liver events with avacopan happened in the first 6 months of treatment, Hellmich said. Of the 22 such events overall, 10 were considered by treating clinicians to be probably or definitely unrelated to the drug. Among the 12 cases considered possibly, probably, or certainly due to avacopan, three continued with their regular dosing and five stopped it temporarily.

Hellmich also emphasized that 20 of the 22 cases had resolved before the interim data cut. One of the other two was reported to have been resolved later, while the last had not but, Hellmich said, was thought to be "clinically irrelevant."

With regard to study limitations, he cautioned that, because site investigators chose treatments based on their own judgments, "residual bias" is a possibility. As well, final results with additional years of treatment might reveal risks not yet apparent.

No, Nissan's Armada isn't getting a name change. Don't freak out, Armada faithful. Instead, as a celebration for the Patrol's 75th anniversary, Nissan is bringing the name back as a trim level on its full-size SUV brute.

Called the Armada Patrol Pro-4X, the body-on-frame SUV adds all sorts of neat off-road extras while also not being terribly different from the normal Pro-4X it replaces, save for new Patrol badging on the tailgate, center console, door sills and floor mats. That's what it's all about, baby. There are also a handful of optional extras, like some very tough-looking Nismo-branded rock sliders and a roof rack with an incorporated light bar, that are new for 2027. They can be had along with Nismo's existing 18-inch Axis wheels, which are wrapped in  BF Goodrich All-Terrain T/A K03 rubber.

Under the hood, you'll find the same twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 as the cool normal Armada, pumping out 425 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque. It's paired to a nine-speed automatic transmission that sends power to all four wheels courtesy of a full-time 4WD system and a locking rear differential. To help keep you out of trouble when you're off-road, the Patrol Pro-4X comes with height-adjustable air suspension, underbody armor, and tow hooks.

If you're the type of person who is a real nasty Nissan nerd, or you just love off-roading, perhaps the 2027 Armada Patrol Pro-4X is for you. If that's the case, you've just got to be ready to fork over $81,265, including $2,275 destination. That's no small chunk of change, but it actually undercuts this car's closest rival, the Toyota Sequoia TRD Pro, by $6,855.

I won't lie to ya, I don't completely understand the decision here for Nissan. I mean, Patrol is hardly an established nameplate in the U.S. It only existed here from 1962 to 1969, and it's been gone for a hell of a long time, so I can't imagine there's a ton of nostalgia behind it. I suppose you could point to an appeal to off-roading nerds as a reason for the name addition or perhaps Nissan is getting ready to switch the Armada's name over to Patrol in the U.S., though I sort of doubt that.

Patrol has been a part of Nissan since 1951, so there's obviously a lot of brand heritage behind it. I'm just not sure there's a lot of brand heritage behind it in the U.S. Better late than never, though, and Patrol Pro-4X does sound a bit cooler than just Pro-4X, so who am I to complain?

#5727. I've Solved The 72-Hour EV Test Drive Conundrum, And Every Automaker Is Free To Steal My Idea (Except Tesla)

Because Republicans have fought so hard to spread pro-oil propaganda about electric vehicles, the general public largely has no idea whether an EV would work for them or not. Batteries easily last well over a decade and are recyclable, fast chargers are actually pretty common, and lifecycle emissions are way lower for EVs even if you account for mining, but somehow, objectively true statements are controversial now. New EV sales in the U.S. are also struggling, and automakers are struggling to find buyers. The good news is, I have an actual, viable solution that automakers are free steal borrow.

OK, so we've seen that spending time living with an EV, even temporarily, goes a long way to debunking pro-oil propaganda and can change people's minds about whether or not an EV is right for them. Personally, I think the easiest way to make that happen is for owners who want to see EVs get more popular to lend their cars to as many people as they can, for at least 3 days at a time. Ideally, automakers would offer 120-hour test drives to anyone who wants one, but that would be wildly expensive, so I understand why it's hard to even get a 72-hour loan.

Automakers can't sit back here, though. And I'm not just saying that because EVs are the future (they really are), or because I want my nieces and nephews to grow up breathing clean air (I really do). No, it's because they're already shipping EVs to the U.S., and selling more of them would help both sales and profits, while keeping excess inventory from piling up on dealer lots. So here's the idea I'm offering every automaker, free and clear: introduce incentives that encourage dealers to use EVs as service loaners.

When an auto journalist gives business advice, usually, the best thing any automaker can do is the opposite. And that goes double when that advice is on Jalopnik, a site that still loves a good s—post. I'm also well aware I'm not a serious journalist. But tell me the service loaner isn't the most cost-effective way to get customers into an EV long enough for them to realize how great it is to have a gas station in your garage.

I know we all love conquest sales, but current owners are your most likely future customers. The real key to a future EV sale, though, is the low-pressure, no-commitment, just-try-it-for-fun nature of the service loaner. Even people who actively hate EVs would probably be willing to play with one for three or four days while their car's in the shop if the loaner was free. Customers are less likely to think it's some sort of sales trick, too, if the offer comes from a service manager instead of a salesperson.

Considering we're talking about people who already own a car, I don't know if we'd see large numbers of owners picking up their cars, handing over the keys to the loaner EV, and demanding to trade their car in. But as long as you make a good car, there are no downsides to making a positive impression on your customers. And I bet that program would end up being the most cost-effective sales tool in any automaker's arsenal. Not because they're forcing people to go electric but because EVs do such a great job of selling themselves when they fit a prospective owner's lifestyle.

Not everyone can justify an EV. It's pricier and less convenient if you can't charge at home, and some people do crazy amounts of driving or frequent towing. But if you work for an automaker, you know your EVs make better daily drivers for regular homeowners than your most popular daily drivers, and you know they'd sell better if you could get more butts in seats. Now you have a way to get your most likely customers' butts in those seats for far less than the cost of launching a 120-hour test drive program.

Even better, the anti-EV crowd should be all over this one. If EVs are still as bad as they're convinced they are, then a few days driving an EV should be all anyone needs to disabuse them of the notion that they should go electric. Give the skeptics at your company the opportunity to rack up a win and prove this whole EV thing is a waste of everyone's time and money. I mean, they aren't afraid people will like EVs better if they just spend some time with one, are they? Let's put our money where our mouth is and find out.

#5726. Trial Stopped Early for Superiority of LBBP-Tuned Pacemakers

— LBBP preserved cardiac function and reduced events for people with AV block in randomized trial

Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) drastically reduced clinical events among patients with atrioventricular (AV) block, with results good enough to stop the OptimPacing trial early.

In that international randomized trial of patients getting permanent pacemakers with high ventricular pacing burden and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) >35%, LBBP bested right ventricular pacing (RVP) when it came to the primary endpoint of combined mortality, heart failure hospitalization, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy at an interim 35.1-month analysis.

The 4-year estimated Kaplan-Meier event rates were 8.5% and 19.2%, respectively (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.23-0.75), reported Jiangang Zou, MD, PhD, of First Affiliated Hospital, Nanjing Medical University, and Westchina Hospital in China. Individual outcomes were also reported for:

Safety-wise, procedure- and pacing system-related complications reached 3.8% and 3.2% in the LBBP and RVP groups, and lead revision occurred in two patients each, Zou reported at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting held in Chicago.

"LBBP demonstrated superiority over RVP in preserving cardiac function and reducing composite clinical outcomes for atrioventricular block," Zou said. "This study provides evidence supporting the consideration of LBBP as a first-line pacing strategy for patients with an anticipated high ventricular pacing requirement."

OptimPacing was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

LBBP is a type of conduction system pacing directly engaging the heart's intrinsic conduction system to preserve left ventricular electrical and mechanical synchrony. The result is typically a lower risk of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy -- compared with forced ventricular pacing -- hence LBBP becoming very popular in real-world practice.

"What we've learned here from this clinical trial, as we've learned when we buy a car or buy a house, is that location, location, location is very important," said Elaine Wan, MD, of Columbia University Medical Center in New York City, discussing the trial during a press conference.

LBBP in OptimPacing meant fixing a 3830 lumenless lead into the interventricular septum until the left ventricular subendocardium was reached, meeting prespecified LBBP criteria, whereas RVP meant a conventional active lead implanted in the right ventricular septum or apex using standard technique.

"Getting there and actually getting the effect, specifically the QRS that is similar to a physiological native QRS, is the goal, so not just parking it there, but actually getting the electrophysiological effect," Wan stressed. From OptimPacing's electrophysiological results of LBBP, "we get the most maintenance and sustainability of ejection fraction so far, since we've known for so long that forced ventricular pacing does not have any beneficial effect."

In 2023, the Heart Rhythm Society guidelines gave cardiac physiologic pacing a class IIa recommendation for patients with an LVEF 36-50% anticipated to require substantial ventricular pacing, and a weaker IIb recommendation for peers with normal LVEF anticipated to require substantial ventricular pacing.

Wan posed the question of whether it's time for a guideline change in the wake of OptimPacing.

"I do think that with the advent of septal left bundle pacing, definitely a lot of electrophysiologists are comfortable with the procedure," she added.

"I think that most of us are using left bundle branch area pacing as the default option," said press conference moderator Cara Pellegrini, MD, of the University of California San Francisco and VA San Francisco. "The rare times that you may still use right atrial right ventricular apical pacing might be if you were struggling with a left bundle area pacing lead and your patient was particularly sick, and you were just trying to do kind of the fastest, most expedient option."

Wan emphasized patient selection and noted that it is also unclear if people with infiltrative heart disease (e.g. amyloidosis) get the same effects from septal LBBP or RVP in someone with a normal heart.

Zou and colleagues conducted the randomized trial in China, Europe, and the U.S. from 2021-2025. The study population consisted of people with an indication for permanent pacemakers with a high ventricular pacing burden, LVEF >35%, and New York Heart Association class I-III symptoms.

Among exclusion criteria were candidates for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or CRT-defibrillator therapy; and people with LVEF 36-50% who were willing to receive biventricular pacing.

The open-label trial had 702 patients randomized and 685 included in the final analysis. The two groups shared balanced baseline characteristics. Mean age was 68.4 years and 57.5% were men. Mean LVEF was 63%, and mean QRS duration about 115 msec. The indication for permanent pacing was atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular rate in 12.7% of the cohort.

Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy was defined as a 10% or larger drop in LVEF and resultant LVEF ≤50% without alternative causes of cardiomyopathy identified. Heart failure hospitalization covered hospital admissions for more than 24 hours with worsening symptoms of heart failure and treatment with IV diuretics or inotropic medications.

LBBP was successfully implanted in 96.8% of patients; left bundle branch capture was confirmed in 87.6%.

The ventricular pacing burden was >90% in both groups.

Left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes were lower with LBBP; LVEF was higher with LBBP.

R-wave sensing and pacing impedance and threshold remained stable in both groups. Left bundle branch capture threshold also remained low and stable, per Zou's report.

Key limitations of OptimPacing include its early termination, which may have led to an overestimation of treatment effects, and the low representation of people with reduced LVEF.

After a Missouri town voted unanimously to cancel its contract with Flock in October, the town, like many others who have recently cancelled contracts, went ahead and covered its flock cameras in black trash bags. Not two weeks later, the town's police department found not only were the cameras still on, but they continued to record vehicles, using infrared technology for the dark trash-bag induced conditions.

Excelsior Springs Police Department took to Facebook on November 5 to inform its residents of the issue. The department's Lieutenant Ryan Dowdy told Local 12 that the city initially placed bags over the cameras when they voted to end its contract with Flock and remove the cameras. However, not only are the cameras still on, the black garbage bags do not seem to block Flock's automated license plate reader's infrared technology. The company touts that tech on its own website as "nighttime performance that doesn't quit."

Also problematic is that with a cancelled contract the police department cannot access or use the data but other law enforcement agencies might be able to.

The 15 cameras installed in the town have recorded some vehicles, Dowdy said that most of these images have been headlights and taillights, with a few license plates. The screenshot image shared to Excelsior Springs Police Department's Facebook page showed a few of the vehicles captured through the garbage bags with the infrared. The third of the semi-hazy images showed a red box over the license plate it captured.

About a month ago, the police department held an informative session with the people of Excelsior Springs to explain Flock's ALPR technology to citizens. Community concerns still prevailed in taking down the cameras, as the council voted unanimously a couple of weeks later to cancel the contract. Although the police department said not using the 15 cameras posted in town will affect its police work, Dowdy said it continues efforts to be honest with area residents.

"You know, we'd rather tell people, be upfront about it," Dowdy said. "We're not trying to hide anything. To be honest, we haven't looked at it until yesterday to even find that it was occurring."

The city's solution for now is to double-bag the cameras until they are removed, hopefully some time around the contract's end at the end of this month. This latest folly is another warning to towns, cities and communities that have gone about covering their cameras with trash bags to double up. Who knows what kind of trash can seep through just the one layer.

#5723. M1/M4 Agonist Relieved Schizophrenia Symptoms in Mid-Stage Trial

— Twice-daily dose hit primary and secondary endpoints

ML-007C-MA, an investigational muscarinic M1/M4 receptor agonist that combines betovumeline and fesoterodine fumarate, significantly improved schizophrenia symptoms in adults who had an acute exacerbation of psychosis, data from the randomized phase II ZEPHYR trial showed.

Those receiving a twice-daily ML-007C-MA dose of 210 mg betovumeline/3 mg fesoterodine fumarate (210/3 mg BID) achieved a statistically significant improvement in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) total score compared with placebo at week 5 (least squares mean difference -4.5 points, P=0.015), reported Kimberly Thompson, PhD, of MapLight Therapeutics, and colleagues.

A once-daily dose of 330 mg betovumeline/6 mg fesoterodine, which delivered lower overall daily exposure, demonstrated numerical improvement over placebo on the primary endpoint but did not achieve statistical significance (-2.8 points, P=0.110).

The findings were presented at the Neuroscience Education Institute (NEI) Fall Congress in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

The 210/3 mg BID dose also met several other key secondary and prespecified endpoints at week 5:

Additionally, participants on the 210/3 mg BID regimen were 2.4 times more likely to achieve a ≥30% reduction in PANSS total score (P=0.021) and 2.8 times more likely to be deemed ready for discharge from an inpatient psychiatric setting by week 5 (P=0.002).

"Despite recent advances in schizophrenia treatment, patients and clinicians continue to need therapies that pair meaningful symptom control with a tolerability profile patients can sustain over time," co-author John Kane, MD, of the Donald and Barbara Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell in New York, said in a company statement.

"The ZEPHYR results are notable on both fronts: a statistically significant improvement on the primary endpoint and cognitive performance, alongside a meaningfully differentiated safety profile that matters most for the management of patients over time," he noted.

ML-007C-MA is an oral, extended-release, fixed-dose combination pairing the investigational M1/M4 agonist betovumeline (ML-007) with fesoterodine fumarate, a peripherally acting muscarinic antagonist. The co-formulation is engineered to sustain central M1/M4 activation in the brain while blocking peripheral cholinergic side effects like nausea, hypersalivation, and gastrointestinal (GI) distress.

By engaging muscarinic rather than dopamine receptors, this mechanism may offer an alternative pathway for patients who are refractory to or intolerant of traditional dopamine-blocking antipsychotics. Xanomeline and trospium chloride (Cobenfy) was the first M1/M4 receptor agonist approved in September 2024, establishing the first novel mechanistic class for schizophrenia in more than three decades.

The 25-site, double-blind trial enrolled 307 participants ages 18 to 64 years with a schizophrenia diagnosis confirmed by the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview. Eligibility criteria required a baseline PANSS total score between 80 and 120, a score of 4 or higher on two or more positive symptom items, a CGI-S score of 4 or higher, and no concurrent antipsychotic therapy.

In the 210/3 mg BID arm, the mean age was 42 years, 70% were male, and 74% identified as Black. Disease severity at baseline was high, reflected by a mean PANSS total score of 96 (on a scale of 30 to 210) and a mean CGI-S score of 5 (on a scale of 1 to 7).

ML-007C-MA was generally well tolerated, with the majority of treatment-emergent adverse events categorized as mild or moderate. No serious or drug-related severe adverse events occurred, and investigators noted an absence of urinary retention, metabolic dysregulation, hepatic liability, or extrapyramidal movement-related signals.

Approximately 7% of participants discontinued treatment due to adverse events (2% attributable to GI issues) compared with 1% in the placebo group.

"No fasting requirement and a one-dose titration support a tolerability profile that is expected to translate into real-world adherence," the researchers noted.

MapLight announced plans to meet with the FDA to discuss phase III trial designs.

#5722. West Yorkshire’s £229 Million Bus Decisions Will Outlast Its Operating Contracts

West Yorkshire has made two substantial commitments to its bus network. On November 2, FirstGroup announced a £109 million agreement with the West Yorkshire Combined Authority covering five depots, associated infrastructure and 330 buses, including 79 battery-electric vehicles. The authority is also spending £120 million on more than 250 new buses through a separate programme. These investments will help establish the region’s new franchised Weaver Network, but many of the assets being acquired will remain in use long after the first operating contracts have ended.

West Yorkshire’s fleet and depot commitments illustrate a problem explored in my 83-page report, The Bus Is Not the System. The accompanying TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines which decisions are becoming expensive to reverse and what authorities should establish before making their next commitments.

The Weaver Network changes the relationship between public transport planning and private bus operations. The Combined Authority will specify services and retain responsibility for passenger revenue under its initial large contracts, while private operators deliver the routes. The region is securing assets that will remain important regardless of which company operates the buses. In principle, that can make future competition easier because bidders do not each have to provide a new depot and fleet.

The challenge is that buses, operating contracts and infrastructure follow different clocks. An operating contract might last five or seven years. Vehicles can work through successive contracts, while depot buildings and electrical connections may remain useful for decades. A change in route patterns, population or employment locations can make an established depot less convenient. A bus can often be reassigned, but a multi-megawatt electricity connection cannot be transferred to another site because the network needs charging capacity elsewhere.

West Yorkshire has arranged a staged transition. The five depot sales have completed, while the buses are scheduled to transfer as new franchises begin operating between May 2027 and October 2028. First Bus will continue delivering existing services under temporary depot leases and will manage electrification at Bradford and Huddersfield, with the authority paying for that work. The arrangements allow services and infrastructure development to proceed while ownership and operating responsibilities change.

Securing strategically important depots is a defensible approach. It reduces dependence on an incumbent operator’s control of scarce infrastructure and can help new companies compete for future contracts. The authority also assumes long-term responsibilities for the assets, including maintenance, future electrical capacity and their suitability for a changing passenger network. A depot can be worth purchasing without every potential alternative having been examined, but the consequences of losing those alternatives should be understood before the agreement becomes binding.

Electrification makes this especially important. Charging equipment, substations and electricity connections involve different suppliers, construction schedules and contractual responsibilities from the buses themselves. Vehicle orders can proceed before chargers are fully commissioned when the infrastructure delivery pathway is sufficiently assured. Problems arise when a fleet commitment depends on electrical capacity that cannot be delivered in time, or when the fallback arrangements are inadequate.

The passenger network can also change in ways that alter the original investment case. Better bus priority can reduce the number of vehicles needed to maintain a timetable. New housing developments can shift demand toward different corridors. A major employment centre or hospital relocation can change the value of existing routes and depots. The infrastructure secured today should support those possibilities rather than make sensible network improvements prohibitively expensive.

None of this argues for delaying every investment until uncertainty disappears. Authorities need to secure land, procure vehicles and obtain electrical connections years before some services begin. The useful distinction is between preparation that reduces uncertainty and commitments that substantially increase the cost of changing direction. Both need to be assessed against the passenger services the authority intends to deliver.

West Yorkshire’s programme offers a concrete example of the opportunity and challenge. Securing assets and specifying passenger services across the metropolitan network may produce a more coherent system than leaving every operator to optimize its own routes and depots. The long-term measure of success will be whether the authority can continue improving that network through changing demand, successive contracts and further electrification without having to reconstruct infrastructure it has already paid to provide.

This assessment concludes my five-part series drawn from The Bus Is Not the System, an 83-page TFIE Strategy report examining four decades of British and Irish metropolitan bus governance. The full West Yorkshire Briefing connects the report’s findings to current fleet, depot, electricity infrastructure and franchising decisions.

#5721. The Power of Schema Markup: A Comprehensive Guide for Real Estate Agents

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. #5720. IIHS Founder Warned Drivers About The Dangers Of Speed Almost A Decade Before He Started The Organization: What's Streaming

Not long before the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety was informing drivers of how dangerous or safe a car was, James S. Kemper was on a mission to improve road safety. Kemper worked in the insurance world in his first job out of high school. He was an "office boy" for Central Mutual Insurance according to his New York Times obituary, but he went on to produce his own driver safety materials: educational films.

The films were made by Kemper's personal insurance company, Lumbermen Mutual Casualty, and in partnership with the LAPD and Traffic Safety Films Inc. The LAPD connection helped bring "Sergeant Bruce" to the films, who starred on-camera several times as the presenter of important safety lessons — each video with its own specific theme. Maybe it's Sgt. Bruce's personality, or maybe it's a cop-thing, but he also delivers a pseudo 1950s-version of scared straight energy with every specific dangerous driving situation.

Join me as I introduce a new(er), sometimes nostalgic video worth adding to your Watch Later lists. Leave a note in the comments if you find an older or interesting film you'd like to see featured.

In "Speed, The Accident Multiplier," a film restored and posted by 16mm Time Machine on YouTube, the on-camera narrator, Sergeant Bruce of the LAPD, explains to viewers that speed is dangerous. He uses charts and figures to show how faster speed increases stopping distances. The biggest takeaway is that the faster you go, the longer it takes to brake, and the more likely the damage to whatever the car hits will be catastrophic. That same messaging carried over into the IIHS organization decades later.

Sgt. Bruce ended the film in a familiar way that you'll find with most of these films: A message about how engaging with these dangers will lead to death. In "Speed," he tells viewers, "Speeding is a two-edged sword. It makes an accident more probable, and at the same time, it makes death more certain." He went on to explain that one out of every three fatal accidents involved a speeding driver, "which means in one out of three cases, a driver took a chance with death and lost."

There are a couple more films Kemper and his organizations had made in 1950 that are also available on YouTube. The next two, or rather four, were uploaded by PeriscopeFilm — specifically, they're two short double-features. The first pairs "Following Too Close" and "Driver Irritations," with the second pairing including "Child Safety" and "Driver or Pedestrian" — with the latter admittedly sounding more like a dangerous game, and that was likely the point. The opening to "Driver or Pedestrian" doesn't mess around either. Within the first minute, a camera follows a man driving a car as Sgt. Bruce tells viewers, "This is a driver..." before cutting to a tombstone, where Sgt. Bruce adds, "...who was a pedestrian. This is how it happened." Quite a way to set the scene.

Nine years later, Kemper's company joined forces with another two insurance companies to form the IIHS. Another decade after that, the IIHS would become its own scientific research organization, conducting studies to better understand road safety and finding ways to help improve it. By that point, IIHS had begun to do its own vehicle safety testing, as well. Those tests — although they have changed some as vehicles have evolved quite a bit since the 1960s — still provide consumers with important information regarding the safety of their vehicles today, like its latest look into the safety of heavy-duty trucks and cargo vans.

Kemper's work in insurance also helped push mutual insurance to the forefront in the U.S., which, if you're unfamiliar, it means the insurance company is owned by policyholders. There are no stock shareholders to appease. He was adamant about ensuring people were paid for their claims. In his New York Times obituary, he's quoted saying, "I made up my mind that this company was going to settle claims for cash in the shortest time possible. I did not see then and do not see now the value of contesting claims you know you will settle." Anyone feel like a few insurance companies could take some notes? Kemper's legacy endures with his insurance company over a century later, which now exists as Kemper Insurance, and the place where he left the biggest mark — in his role establishing the IIHS.

#5719. Autism Risk Myths: 1 in 4 Adults Cite Vaccines or Tylenol

— Beliefs tied to political affiliation, survey of 30,000 Americans showed

About one in four U.S. adults endorsed childhood vaccinations or acetaminophen (Tylenol) use during pregnancy as an autism risk factor, a cross-sectional study showed.

In a nationwide survey of 30,000 adults, 26.6% endorsed the vaccination belief and 23.1% endorsed the acetaminophen belief, reported Roy Perlis, MD, MSc, of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, and co-authors in JAMA Health Forum.

Genetic causes, an evidence-based risk factor, was the most widely endorsed, at 66.7%.

Political affiliation was strongly associated with vaccination beliefs. In adjusted models, adults who identified as strong Republicans had 3.83 (95% CI 3.47-4.24) times the odds of endorsing the vaccine-autism belief compared with strong Democrats.

Vaccine-autism risk beliefs were highest among adults ages 35 to 44 years (adjusted OR 1.64 compared with those ages 18 to 24 years), and lowest among people 65 and older (adjusted OR 0.64).

Greater trust in scientific and medical institutions was associated with lower rates of endorsement, as was more frequent social media use.

"Our results add to abundant evidence of the growing politicization of beliefs about science and medicine," Perlis and co-authors stated. "This politicization of science preceded the COVID-19 pandemic, but variability in responses to the pandemic by state and federal leadership likely accelerated this trend."

Prior survey results have documented a decline in trust in healthcare and science during the pandemic, they noted. "Our results may reflect this diminished trust in traditional sources of public health information," Perlis and colleagues observed.

"This study documents the corrosive effect of the epidemic of disinformation that has been promoted by a range of government officials and others to foster false beliefs about vaccines," said Georges Benjamin, MD, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C., who wasn't involved with the research.

"It shows we have a lot a work to do as an evidence-based field to turn this around," Benjamin told MedPage Today.

"What is especially concerning is the preponderance of these false beliefs among people of different political parties," he pointed out. "Science is supposed to be apolitical, but this shows the negative impact of the politicization of health information."

In 1998, a case series published in The Lancet suggested vaccination was associated with autism risk; the paper was retracted after numerous flaws were identified. Since then, large population-based studies have consistently showed no link between vaccines and autism.

"There has been no subsequent credible evidence supporting a link, whereas numerous studies have demonstrated no such association," Perlis and co-authors wrote. However, both President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have repeatedly suggested vaccines could play a role in rising autism rates.

Maternal acetaminophen use also has been suggested to increase autism risk despite strong evidence against a link, the researchers noted. In September 2025, Trump tied prenatal acetaminophen use to autism, warning pregnant women of possible risks.

To assess the potential effect of this type of information on the public, Perlis and colleagues evaluated data from an internet-based survey of adults ages 18 or older in all 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia. The survey was administered between December 18, 2025, and January 27, 2026.

The primary study outcome was the endorsement of individual risk factors, scored on a 5-point Likert scale from definitely false to definitely true. Among the 30,288 survey respondents in the analysis, the mean age was 46.6 years. Most (54.1%) identified as women, 45.2% as men, and 0.6% as nonbinary.

Endorsement of vaccine-autism risk beliefs was associated with men (adjusted OR 1.26), and African American or Black (adjusted OR 1.25) or Hispanic (adjusted OR 1.13) respondents compared with white respondents.

Adults who used social media multiple times a day had lower odds of endorsing misinformation (adjusted OR 0.72 compared with those who used it less than weekly).

"Although social media use has been blamed for accelerating dissemination of misinformation, we did not identify a positive association between social media use and belief in non-evidence-based risk factors," Perlis and co-authors noted. "One possibility is that social media use parallels information seeking more generally -- i.e., those with lower levels of use are also those with less access to sources of reliable health information."

The analysis was cross-sectional and causality cannot be determined, the researchers noted. Social media use was self-reported and may not have been accurate.

#5716. A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body

A single sauna session may trigger a surprising response in the immune system. Researchers in Finland have discovered that spending just 30 minutes in a sauna, with a brief cold shower halfway through, causes white blood cells to surge into the bloodstream. These cells are essential to the body's defenses, helping identify and fight infections and other potential threats.

The findings suggest that sauna bathing may temporarily mobilize immune cells that normally remain in tissues, allowing them to circulate more widely throughout the body. This increased movement could help the immune system monitor for harmful pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.

During the study, researchers observed an increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured. Among them were neutrophils and lymphocytes, two important groups of immune cells. Neutrophils are often among the first defenders to respond to an infection, while lymphocytes include cells that recognize specific threats, produce antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses.

The increase was temporary. Within 30 minutes after the sauna session, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts had returned to their original levels.

How Sauna Bathing May Activate Immune Defenses

"This may indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes additional white blood cells into the bloodstream from tissues, where they are then redeposited after the session. This kind of periodic release of white blood cells into the bloodstream is beneficial, as once they leave their storage sites, they are better able to patrol the body and respond to pathogens," says Ilkka Heinonen, an Academy Research Fellow at the University of Turku.

This process is known as immune surveillance. Rather than remaining in one location, immune cells travel through the bloodstream and tissues, searching for signs of infection or other abnormalities. By temporarily increasing the number of white blood cells in circulation, the body may improve their ability to detect potential threats.

Interestingly, a similar response occurs during physical exercise. Exercise can temporarily increase the number of immune cells moving through the bloodstream, helping distribute them throughout the body. The new findings suggest that sauna bathing may produce a comparable short-term response, although this does not mean the two activities provide identical immune benefits.

Sauna Heat Also Affects Immune Signaling Molecules

The researchers also investigated whether sauna bathing influenced cytokines, small proteins that help immune cells communicate with one another. Cytokines play important roles in regulating inflammation, coordinating immune defenses, and directing the body's response to infections.

Overall, the sauna session produced little change in average cytokine levels in the bloodstream. However, a closer examination revealed an interesting connection between certain cytokines and changes in body temperature.

"Interestingly, however, the levels of several cytokines changed in relation to how much body temperature rose during sauna bathing. No similar association was observed between white blood cell counts and changes in body temperature," says Professor Jari Laukkanen, who led the study at the University of Eastern Finland.

In other words, some immune signaling molecules responded differently depending on how much a person's body temperature increased. White blood cell counts, however, did not show the same relationship with rising body temperature.

This distinction suggests that sauna bathing may influence different parts of the immune system through different physiological processes.

What This Discovery Means for Sauna Health Benefits

Previous research has linked regular sauna bathing with several potential health benefits. The latest findings offer another clue about what may be happening inside the body during these sessions, particularly how heat exposure and the sauna routine affect immune cell circulation.

However, the researchers caution that the results do not establish whether sauna bathing produces lasting improvements in immune function or reduces the risk of illness. The study examined only the immediate effects of one sauna session, and the observed changes in white blood cells were short-lived.

Because the session also included a brief cold shower, the findings reflect the combined sauna and cooling routine rather than the isolated effects of heat alone.

The research involved 51 adults with an average age of 50. The findings were published in the scientific journal Temperature, which specializes in research on body temperature regulation and its effects on human physiology.

Although more research is needed to understand the long-term implications, the study reveals that even a single sauna session can rapidly change how immune cells circulate through the body, potentially offering new insight into the biological effects of this popular relaxation practice.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5714. Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990

Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5713. Feud Between Former Trump Officials Exposes Divisions Over MAHA Movement

— Blowup began when Calley Means accused officials of catering to lobbyists

A public spat between former Trump administration officials over alleged corruption in public health policymaking is the latest front in Republicans' postelection recriminations, a battle that has exposed fault lines within the White House and could reshape political alliances involving the influential Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement.

The blowup began when Calley Means, a former top advisor to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the MAHA movement, appeared on Joe Rogan's podcast Friday and accused Susie Wiles, James Blair, and others of catering to foreign and domestic lobbyists at the expense of Americans' health.

Wiles, who was recently replaced as White House chief of staff, and Blair, a top political advisor, have denied the allegations.

Means' remarks came days after voters cast ballots in midterm elections where government corruption was among the top issues for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress.

The issue overlaps with concerns from MAHA activists, who have been focused on combating what they see as systemic and harmful corporate influence over policymaking. MAHA became an important part of Trump's coalition after Kennedy endorsed him during the last presidential campaign, and fractures could create political headaches or new avenues for congressional investigations in the coming years.

Zen Honeycutt, a former Kennedy campaign staffer and founder of the group Moms Across America, said Means is "amplifying the frustrations that a lot of MAHA folks have had the past few months and validating them." She's "excited for a new beginning" now that Trump has replaced Wiles with Stephen Miller, whom she views as more aligned with the movement.

But Honeycutt hasn't ruled out working with Democrats, such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom she met with in July to discuss shared environmental priorities, including the pesticide glyphosate and artificial intelligence data centers.

"The MAHA movement does not belong to any party or politician," Honeycutt said.

Means Alleges Outside Interests Influenced Policymaking

On Rogan's show, Means recounted a conversation he had with Wiles about her declining to support certain MAHA initiatives because she needed donations from the sugar industry. "Calley, we can't do this. I need sugar money," he recalled Wiles saying to him. "I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms."

"There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for," Means said. Rogan's show was released Friday, shortly before Trump announced Wiles would step down as White House chief of staff.

Means was hired as a White House advisor early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation's leading physician groups, federal agencies, and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests. Means left the Trump administration in October, without stating a reason for his exit.

"She has taken a stranglehold on any policy decision" impacting the MAHA movement, alongside her former lobbying firm Ballard Partners, Means said about Wiles.

Referring to Blair in the Rogan interview, Means said he has "explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters." He said he believed much of what he was alleging "happened without Trump's full knowledge."

Blair, who previously served as a White House deputy chief of staff before taking an outside role in Trump's political operation, responded on social media that he was contemplating suing Means over his statements.

In text messages between Means and Blair, viewed by the Associated Press, Blair told Means "if you get near slandering or defaming me I will sue you," and "if you are gonna try to knife me, I'm happy to return the favor."

The White House denied Means' accusations.

"The Trump Administration has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said.

Brian Ballard, founder of Ballard Partners, denied communicating with top White House officials on glyphosate and other issues in a statement posted on social media.

The extraordinary public fight, which was continuing on social media Monday, comes after MAHA had grown disenchanted over some of the administration's moves.

In recent months, many grassroots MAHA activists who had initially hoped to collaborate with Trump's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had soured on the agency and the administration, viewing them as infiltrated by lobbyist interests.

They pointed to various insiders in the agricultural and chemical industries who'd secured high-level positions in the EPA and blamed them for the administration's failure to pass meaningful reforms to address microplastics in drinking water or pesticides on farms.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin promised last December to unveil a formal agenda of MAHA policies he would act on. But by the summer, the so-called MAHA agenda had never surfaced, and an EPA spokesperson told the AP that MAHA is an ongoing effort, rather than a single report.

That apparent reversal prompted several activists to say they planned to vote on issues over party in November's elections.

"People are done with the profits of corporations being prioritized over public health," Alexandra Muñoz, PhD, a molecular toxicologist who collaborates with MAHA activists on certain issues, told the AP in July. "And I think that will have an important role in the midterms."

The simmering MAHA frustration, coupled with Means' allegations, could put MAHA support in play for Democrats, something Means himself suggested over the weekend.

"There's a lot of complicated issues that I'm sure Democrats are going to want to address. But when it comes to these issues on MAHA, I think there is huge opportunity in the next year to get some big things done," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

But doing so poses its own complications.

Democrats who will take over both chambers of Congress next year could use Means' statements as a vehicle to begin investigations into White House officials. Some Democrats have long sought to investigate Kennedy over his upending of vaccine policy and his vast cuts to science research, among other decisions. Pushing hard against Kennedy, however, could complicate efforts to build closer ties with MAHA supporters, many of whom still view the health secretary positively.

Means' interviews included a profuse defense of Kennedy, who some have speculated could attempt another run for president in 2028. Means called Kennedy a "hero" on the podcast interview.

#5712. A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms

Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.

Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.

The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.

A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms

To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.

Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.

The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.

These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.

A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality

"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.

The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.

The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).

"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."

Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?

Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.

Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.

"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.

However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.

"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.

If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.

#5711. Court blocks CMS' moratorium on new ACA broker registrations

Court blocks CMS' moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act."

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters."

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment."

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them."

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#5710. Early Response to MASH Drug Linked to Resolution, Fibrosis Improvement

— Noninvasive blood and imaging biomarkers could be signal of response without need for biopsy

In patients treated with resmetirom (Rezdiffra), early responses in blood and imaging biomarkers were associated with resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis improvement, according to an exploratory analysis of the phase III MAESTRO-NASH trial.

Pooled data across treatment and placebo arms showed that these markers at weeks 12 to 16 correlated with MASH resolution and fibrosis improvement responses at week 52. Odds ratios ranged from 2.03 to 8.83 for alanine aminotransferase (ALT), magnetic resonance elastography liver stiffness measurement (MRE LSM), and MRI-proton density fat fraction (PDFF; all P≤0.001).

Responses in PRO-C3 -- a biomarker of active fibrogenesis regularly used in clinical trials -- also were associated with week-52 MASH resolution and fibrosis improvement, reported Rohit Loomba, MD, of the University of California San Diego, at the annual Liver Meeting in Denver, sponsored by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases.

Not surprisingly, the odds of achieving biomarker responses increased with resmetirom versus placebo.

With these biomarkers that are clinically available today, "these associations remain significant even after adjusting for weight loss," Loomba said.

He observed that these early changes in blood and imaging biomarkers could give clinicians a noninvasive signal of response to resmetirom without an invasive biopsy.

During a Q&A session after the presentation, David Goldberg, MD, of the Miller School of Medicine at the University of Miami, said that while the data are impressive, "we can't ignore the elephant in the room about the data integrity concerns" -- a reference to a whistleblower lawsuit from Michael Charlton, MD, a former senior vice president and head of clinical development at Madrigal Pharmaceuticals, that recently became public. Charlton claims that the company, which developed resmetirom, forced him to resign after he raised safety concerns about the drug. Madrigal disputes the allegations.

In explaining the rationale behind the exploratory analysis, Loomba noted that the FDA granted accelerated approval to resmetirom -- a liver-directed thyroid hormone receptor-β selective agonist -- for the treatment of patients with noncirrhotic MASH with stages F2 and F3 fibrosis, in conjunction with diet and exercise.

The approval was based on results from MAESTRO-NASH, which showed treatment with the drug increased rates of MASH resolution and improvement in fibrosis versus placebo at week 52.

"Treatment response was confirmed by liver biopsy in the trial, but in clinical practice we typically do not perform liver biopsy to assess treatment response," Loomba pointed out. "So the key question we are trying to understand here is, in a patient taking resmetirom, what early treatment-related changes in biomarkers or imaging are associated with histologic response at week 52?"

Loomba and his colleagues also found that patients on resmetirom had a shortened time to sustained response across all four of these tests.
