#5601. SERHANT. Latest Brokerage to Join American Real Estate Association

The American Real Estate Association (ARA) on Nov. 9 announced that SERHANT., founded by celebrity agent Ryan Serhant, famous for his Manhattan-based reality TV show, has joined the national trade association.

Since expanding beyond New York in 2023, SERHANT. has grown to 20 states and Washington, D.C., including 2026 launches in California, Texas, Colorado, Massachusetts and Illinois.

ARA, according to a release, is focused on elevating professional standards and the value real estate agents deliver to the public. The release touted Serhant’s brand and global media network, claiming more than 11 million followers, as something that helps expand ARA’s national footprint and strengthens its platform.

“When we launched ARA, our mission was clear: build a unified voice of reason, an association by agents, for agents, that relentlessly fights for the industry,” said Jason Haber and Mauricio Umansky, co-founders of ARA, in a joint statement. “Attaching Ryan Serhant and SERHANT. into this mission is a major step forward. It shows that this industry belongs to true professionals who are fiercely dedicated to their clients and to delivering the highest level of service.”

Asked if ARA is also seeking out partnerships with smaller brokerages or getting involved in other local/state advocacy outside of New York and Missouri, Haber told RISMedia that “we are hearing from many smaller firms in the Midwest, as an example, and we are just as excited to meet with them as we were to meet with SERHANT. Not every firm will make headlines by signing up with us, but we are thrilled to work with them as well.

“There is clearly a hunger, excitement and enthusiasm across this country for a new voice in the industry. In November alone we rolled out our State Chair program, our licensee-in-the-loop legislation and our AI taskforce. Later this month we are giving back to the community by feeding 3,000 people for Thanksgiving. It’s a big month for us at ARA.”

Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT., as well as a broker, author and the star and executive producer of Netflix’s “Owning Manhattan,” said that “ARA is doing the hard work to raise the bar for the entire profession while fighting for homeownership across the country. Aligning SERHANT. with ARA gives our agents an even stronger platform to educate consumers, advocate for clients and shape where this industry goes next.”

“The rapid convergence of industry leaders under ARA’s umbrella shows how hungry the market was for modern, agent-first leadership,” said Briggs Elwell, co-founder and CEO of RLTYco and a member of ARA’s board of directors. “Pairing ARA’s advocacy and education with powerhouses like SERHANT. empowers agents to operate as true, highly skilled business owners.”

SERHANT. joins Compass International Holdings, REMAX and Douglas Elliman among the major firms that have aligned with ARA. This year the association expanded its board of directors with Chris Lim, the former president and chief growth officer of REMAX, and investor Andrew Dodge, who serve alongside Douglas Elliman President and CEO Michael Liebowitz, Douglas Elliman General Counsel Deva Roberts and Elwell.

ARA also continues to bring national weight to state fights. In August, Missouri voters rejected Amendments 4 and 5, ballot measures ARA opposed alongside the Missouri Association of Realtors®.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5600. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5599. Donna Kelce Sells Florida Condo for $485K—Less Than a Year After Major Makeover

NFL matriarch Donna Kelce has offloaded her newly renovated Florida condo for $485,000—less than a year after carrying out a complete overhaul of the pad.

In March, it was revealed that the 74-year-old mother of NFL stars Travis and Jason Kelce had embarked on a major overhaul of her Orlando abode, hiring a local company to replace multiple windows and doors throughout the two-bedroom property.

The project sparked an over-the-top response from fans of the famous football family, and led to Donna's sons calling out the reaction in an episode of their podcast, "New Heights," during which they mocked their mother over the work, joking that she was attempting to turn her condo into a "gilded palace."

However, the renovations seemed to make a big difference when it came to selling the home, with TMZ reporting that the property has found a new owner.

Donna has owned the 1,434-square-foot property since 2019, when she purchased the residence for $355,000. The condo, which was built in 2005, features a wraparound balcony, a den, library, home office, and workout room.

The mom of two previously spoke out about the renovation in a candid interview with Architectural Digest, telling the outlet that work was completed on her home—while setting the record straight about the changes that were made to the dwelling.

"It’s a lot of windows because I’m on the side of the building. So there’s like 16 windows, and they’re floor-length, and it was quite a project," she shared, before hitting back at reports that she'd needed to replace six doors during the renovation.

"The windows that are floor-length along the balcony, they call all of them doors, but they weren’t," she stated. "There were only two doors. But there were six of those [in total], and two of them had handles on them."

As for the viral response to her renovation news, Donna admitted that it "took [her] by surprise," adding: "I was kind of taken off guard."

At the time, Donna revealed she was looking forward to relaxing inside the updated space, explaining that she's happily settled into her routine in the property, where she lives alone, having divorced her former spouse, Ed, soon after their sons finished college.

Addressing her daily routine at home, the proud grandma said she begins each day with coffee, before figuring out what's on her agenda—and confirming whether or not it will require her to go to the airport.

Her children are also a big priority, she said, noting that, while they are both "so busy, it's almost impossible" to speak to them every day, she does her best to check in as often as she can.

"Especially in the offseason, I have no idea what city they’re in [or] where they’re going. But they’re always on my mind," she said.

She admitted that much of her relaxation time revolves around her favorite gadget in the house—her television—which she regularly eats her meals in front of, noting that she "doesn't really care what anybody thinks" about her habits, particularly because she lives alone.

"It connects you to the world. It allows you to relax. Not only that, but it’s important to have to learn about the news and what’s going on in the world," she added.

Donna said she will occasionally fall asleep with the TV on, but sets a timer to ensure that she isn't snoozing in front of the screen for longer than 20 minutes.

And while she seems fairly relaxed about her life at home, the mother of two admitted that she does have one very clear rule for guests who visit: no pets allowed on the furniture.

"I don’t have any pets. I think a person’s home is their home, and if that’s where they want their pet, have at it. If it’s in my house, no. But most people that I know of who have animals allow their pets on the furniture," she explained.

In addition to being a place Donna can relax, she said her condo was also packed with precious reminders of her sons' success—and the incredible experiences she has enjoyed as a result of their hard work.

“There are so many [photos]. So many pictures of all the amazing people that I've been able to meet, all the wonderful places that I've been able to go, all the games, all the Super Bowls,” Donna shared.

“It's more than a mother should ever hope for. I can't even tell you how full of love and admiration [I am] for my kids to be able to give that to our family.”

Donna's dwelling first shot into the headlines back in March, when TMZ revealed that she was carrying out construction work at the home. Her sons then added further fuel to the fire when they raised it as a topic of conversation on "New Heights."

Addressing the furor surrounding the renovations on their podcast that same week, Travis and Jason joked to their listeners: "Let's talk about the most important news out of the Kelce family this week. We wanted to break this news on the show, but reports have already started to leak out."

"Donna Kelce is remodeling her modest Florida home! Let's give it up for Donna!" Jason added.

The siblings then brought Donna in to share her thoughts on the media response to her renovation plans—with the NFL matriarch admitting that she had been stunned by the attention it received.

"Even TMZ sent me a text and said, 'Can you be honest, it's really funny!' I'm like ... it's so stupid!" she said, before attempting to play down the work she's having done.

"All they're doing is, people are coming to put in my windows on Monday," she continued. "You know my whole apartment is all windows. It's windows all the way around."

Still, Jason couldn't help but get in another joke, asking: "Are you going to bulletproof?"

Undeterred, Donna continued by explaining that the unseasonably cold weather in Orlando had motivated her to replace the existing window designs, because they were "cheap" and outdated, providing little protection against the chill.

"This year, it got so cold down here—it was in the 30s—and I literally had sweat coming down the windows and pools of water in my living room because it couldn't handle it. These are cheap windows that were put in 20 years ago," she shared.

Jason then called out TMZ's description of Donna's property as a "modest home," joking that she appears to have plans to turn it into a much swankier abode.

"Well, I just wanted to say, 'Mom, they said "modest home," and it just feels like you're turning this place into a bit of a gilded palace,'" he said.

#5598. Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features

Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million.

The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX Agent Cloud, a service that artificial intelligence agents can use to store their data. Dropbox is also adding new AI productivity features to its flagship file sharing platform.

Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris Data offers an object storage service that runs across multiple public clouds. The company says that it enables applications to read and write several times faster than competing offerings. Furthermore, the service includes several features designed to optimize AI workloads.

AI agents often run in sandboxes that include, among other resources, the data they need to carry out their work. Loading data into a sandbox can be a relatively time-consuming process, which slows agent performance. Tigris Data offers a feature called bucket forms that speeds up the workflow. Furthermore, it prevents agents from modifying information that is used by other workloads.

Tigris Data’s service monitors the locations from which agents access records. When it detects a new location, it moves a copy of the records to a nearby server in order to reduce latency. The service caches the most frequently used files on high-speed storage infrastructure to further reduce access times.

Dropbox said Tigris Data will support its push into the AI infrastructure market. The company debuted its first entry into that product category, DBX Agent Cloud, in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Like Tigris Data’s service, it’s an S3-compatible object storage offering optimized for AI agents.

The storage stalwart plans to add a file system capability further down the line. Object storage is best suited for unstructured datasets, while file systems are used to store records that are organized into folders. Dropbox plans to release the technology alongside “content processing capabilities.” The company says that those features will make it easier for AI models to process information kept in DBX Agent Cloud.

The offering is rolling out alongside a major overhaul of Dropbox’s flagship file sharing platform. An enhanced search bar will enable users to look for images by entering a description of the file they seek.

Furthermore, Dropbox can now respond to questions about a file by generating a natural language summary. A worker could, for example, request an overview of the changes that colleagues have made to an important folder over the past week.

Dropbox can not only edit questions about files but also edit them. The company says that users can have the built-in AI models change a file’s format, move it to a different folder or combine it with other records into a PDF document. Several other actions are supported as well. Users can mix and match actions into multistep workflows.

The new AI productivity features are initially available to customers in the U.S., the U.K. and Australia with Standard and Advanced subscriptions. Dropbox plans to expand access next year.

#5597. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

#5596. Columbia, South Carolina, Balances Growth and Affordability Challenges

Columbia remains a market defined by competing forces. Demand fundamentals continue to support housing activity, but elevated home prices, affordability pressures, and a cooler sales environment are creating some new challenges for builders operating in the region.

The market’s long-term outlook remains supported by solid demographic trends. Columbia’s population is approaching 890,000 residents, while household growth continues to outpace many mature markets. Household formation is expected to remain positive through 2028, providing a steady stream of potential buyers and renters. Meanwhile, median household income continues to rise, helping support housing demand even as affordability remains strained.

Adding to the area’s economic foundation is the presence of the University of South Carolina, which enrolled more than 40,000 students in 2025. According to a university study, the institution generates billions in annual economic activity across the region through payroll, purchases, and tax contributions.

While market conditions have cooled from the rapid growth period seen earlier in the decade, Columbia remains structurally undersupplied. Zonda’s analysis indicates the market is currently undersupplied by roughly 3.7%, suggesting that long-term housing demand still exceeds available inventory.

Builders have responded by expanding community offerings. Active projects increased year over year, with 109 communities currently operating across the market. At the same time, quick move-in inventory remains relatively manageable, signaling that builders have largely avoided excessive speculative inventory buildup.

Like most other markets across the country, affordability remains one of the market’s biggest hurdles. Columbia’s housing market is currently considered overvalued relative to local income levels, with home prices continuing to exceed income-supported pricing.

Still, the broader economic backdrop remains supportive. Employment levels continue to grow, unemployment remains relatively low, and household growth is forecast to continue over the next several years. Combined with the market’s ongoing housing deficit, those factors should help sustain demand even as affordability challenges limit the pace of future growth.

#5594. Russell Brand Moved to Florida Months Before British Police Formally Charged Him With Rape

British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to over 10 years behind bars—more than a year after he relocated his entire family to Florida to escape "attacks" by the "media, government, and judiciary."

According to the New York Times, a London court found Brand, 51—who was previously married to pop star Katy Perry, and now shares three children with wife Laura Brand—guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and not guilty of two additional counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," Judge Joel Bennathan said while handing down the sentence in a London court on Nov. 9.

Following an April 2025 arrest by Metropolitan Police, Brand denied all charges, sharing a video statement on his X account, in which he insisted that he has "never engaged in non-consensual activity," while conceding that he had acted like "a fool" when he was "young and single."

"I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family, who were just about a shot over there, my beautiful children, I was a fool, man," he said in the video, which appears to have been shot in Florida.

The alleged offenses are understood to involve six women and took place between 1999 and 2009. Police interviewed Brand about the allegations—which were first brought to light in 2023, when The Sunday Times and Channel 4, two British media outlets, released an expose in which Brand's accusers claimed they had been assaulted or raped by the comedian.

Brand vehemently denied all accusations of "non-consensual activity" at the time.

He is understood to have moved his family from their home in Oxfordshire in favor of a rental property in the Sunshine State, where he is reportedly living in a $2.5 million home in Santa Rosa Beach.

Although he has not revealed when exactly he moved, it has been reported by multiple outlets that he relocated shortly before the 2024 presidential election. Images taken of the comedian show him enjoying public events in the Santa Rosa Beach area as early as October of that year.

The Times reported in 2025 that Brand, his wife, and their three children had been living in a $3.3 million home in the U.K. before their move. It is unclear if they have since sold it.

Brand has also not confirmed whether he is planning to purchase a home in the U.S., where he is currently renting a property.

In the lead-up to his move, the comedian and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" star had been making efforts to connect with members of now-President Donald Trump's inner circle, interviewing Donald Trump Jr. at his Florida home in 2024 and attending a black-tie dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where he received a Global Defender of Freedom Award.

In April 2025, Brand sat down for an in-depth interview with Fox News host—and newly minted Florida resident—Sean Hannity, during which he opened up about his past addictions and his Christian faith.

Since moving to Santa Rosa Beach, the comedian has reportedly been seen attending church services, as well as yoga sessions, with one local telling The Sun that Brand "always says hello" when they see him.

It is not the first time that Brand has resided in the U.S., having previously owned multiple properties in Los Angeles—including a $6.5 million Mediterranean-style home in the Hollywood Hills, which he shared with Perry, his wife at the time.

Before that, he was reported to have been living in a 1920s abode nearby, which he purchased for $2.2 million in 2013.

Most recently, he snapped up a three-bedroom, five-bathroom Spanish-style property, also in the Hollywood Hills, this time paying $3 million.

The home, which Brand bought in 2019, was built in 1956. The original listing noted that it had since undergone several renovations. He put that property on the market for $3.5 million in summer 2024.

#5593. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5592. Atomicwork launches certified AI coworker marketplace for enterprise IT and security

Information technology service management startup Atomicwork Inc. today announced the launch of an Artificial Intelligence Coworker Marketplace that will give enterprise IT and security teams access to prebuilt, certified AI coworkers that can work alongside employees.

The company said these agentic AI coworkers include verified roles and capabilities across cloud infrastructure, access management, security and device operations.

“Most AI-native ITSM vendors today don’t have much to show for their agents’ effectiveness — a listing means ‘this agent works,’ not ‘this AI Agent has real, verified coverage of the systems it needs to touch and has been tested and fine-tuned using real-world enterprise use cases,’ which has made enterprises wary of agentic claims,” co-founder and Chief Executive Vijay Rayapati told SiliconANGLE.

Founded in 2022, Atomicwork began with the premise that information technology and security teams face challenging, process-intensive work and long tasks that could be automated. To tackle these problems, the company evaluated its agentic coworkers against real enterprise use cases, giving organizations a faster way to deploy AI workers without developing or validating them from scratch.

The initial lineup of coworkers includes an enterprise operations AI coworker, along with a CloudOps engineer, AccessOps manager, SecOps manager and DeviceOps manager. These AI coworkers can work across enterprise systems including AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, Okta, Active Directory, Splunk and Google SecOps.

The company said every AI Coworker comes out of the box with the skills and integrations needed for its role, reducing the work IT teams would otherwise spend wiring up systems and validating procedures.

Every agent can be quickly tailored to internal infrastructure, company culture, specialized expertise and business logic. Using that, they can quickly generate and tackle large volumes of recurring operational work under the supervision of IT and security teams. The company added that administrators will retain full control of agent management, allowing them to decide what systems an agent can access, what actions it can perform and how those actions are governed.

The objective is not merely to provide a catalog of available agents with a card to explain their capabilities. Atomicwork’s certification verifies that each AI Coworker has the needed integrations and skill coverage for the role to get the work done before deployment.

Atomicwork said customers using access automation have already seen speed-ups, with applications that don’t require approval having a median turnaround of about 18 seconds, while those requiring approval have a turnaround of about 2.5 hours. In contrast, the industry standard, which can be heavily influenced by business maturity and the risk behind the application’s use, could take between a full day and three business days depending on the amount of automation behind the scenes.

The company said this marketplace represents the beginning of a broader plan to create an ecosystem of enterprise AI Coworkers, built and certified by Atomicwork. Third parties will also be able to contribute skills and integrations through its Model Context Protocol store and skill registry to enhance coworker capabilities.

“This launch is the first step toward a third-party AI Coworker marketplace, where partners publish their own coworkers and certify them against our enterprise bench,” said Rayapati.

#5591. The 2027 Paint Colors of the Year Take an Emotional Turn

In the past, one hue typically dominated paint colors of the year, with different brands interpreting the color. For 2027, while there are a few blues and greens on offer, there is a much wider variety. Themes are less color-specific and more about emotional intent.

“Color has always been tied to emotion. We instinctively use it to create spaces that make us feel a certain way, and the colors we choose often reflect what we’re looking for in our lives,” says Lisbeth Parada, color marketing manager for Dutch Boy and Minwax brands.

​In 2027, that’s digital detox, permission to be authentic, and the opportunity for stillness and reflection.

​“We’re living in a world increasingly shaped by technology, algorithms, and an almost constant stream of information telling us what to think, what to buy, and how to live. We sense a growing desire to reconnect with our own instincts and the tangible experiences that make us feel human,” says Phillipa Radon, interior designer and C2 paint color specialist.

This year’s color trends tell us it’s not enough to treat home as a retreat anymore; recharging is necessary too, to manage the fast pace of the world around us. The variety of colors suggests multiple ways to gather that energy, with consumers choosing what resonates with them.

In new-construction homes, color choice is even more important, with paint offering homeowners a powerful way to personalize a brand-new space and forge that emotional connection to restoration.

​Here are the paint colors of the year for 2027.

​Sometimes paint color names are intentionally vague as part of their marketing micro-story. Not BEHR’s Grounded, with a name and a mossy green color that instantly frame the experience.

Its name has a double meaning too, as an invitation to breathe and get back to basics, amid digital overwhelm.

“What makes Grounded so relevant as BEHR’s 2027 Color of the Year is the way it balances two things people increasingly want from their homes: calm, and a feeling of life,” says Kayla Kratz, head of color at BEHR.

She notes that for many years, that meant paring down to a minimalist aesthetic, but today’s homeowners want more warmth and personality.

“Grounded answers that shift. The moss and olive tones bring a natural vitality, while warm brown undertones add depth and steadiness. The result is restorative without being static.”

Kratz says that the color replicates the dynamic greens of a forest, evolving throughout the day and changing light conditions.

​Deep Rooted, a nature-inspired warm orange, is energetic but steady and reassuring.

​“There’s an optimistic quality to the color. It has enough richness and energy to support bold contrasts and individual expression. The name brings those ideas together: feeling rooted while remaining open to possibility, and Deep Rooted captures that balance,” says Parada.

​It’s a perfect example of how paint color names are shaping the experience this year, with this color meant to encourage strength by standing still, not always easily done in today’s fast pace of living.

“​The paint color name captures both the color’s connection to nature and the sense of grounding many people want their homes to provide. At home, that translates into spaces that feel personal, welcoming, and comfortably lived in,” says Parada.

​Artifact is a smoky, atmospheric blue intended to create space to pause, recalibrate, and think more clearly after you’ve had a chance to catch your breath. These moments in time are both treasured and rare, which is reflected in the paint color name.

Artifact also embraces the idea of authorship, and how major change doesn’t necessarily require a makeover.

​“As consumers move away from creating homes that look like everyone else’s, they’re focusing on spaces that reflect who they are, where they’ve been, and what matters most to them, “ says Ashley McCollum, color marketing manager at Glidden.

​“People don’t necessarily want to reinvent themselves or start from scratch but rather make thoughtful adjustments that help their life feel more balanced and manageable,” says McCollum.

​“Artifact is not a reinvention, but a readjustment. It brings a sense of ease and relaxation after a busy day, helping you to unwind and feel more grounded. As a mid-tone, smoky blue, it leans warmer and has depth that strikes a balance between focus and comfort.”

This calming blue is nuanced and versatile, the kind of color that’s felt before it is seen, making it a good choice for homeowners who are choosing colors for an emotional impact.

Celery is a light green with yellow undertones that feels more herbal than botanical. It’s fresh and lively, marking a transition for Sherwin-Williams’ color trends.

Their paint color of the year last year was Universal Khaki, inspired by nostalgia and the comfort found in familiarity. Celery takes that feel-good energy into the future on a positive note. The color emerges alongside consumers’ appetite for expressive colors and a continued focus on wellness design.

A few paint colors of the year for 2027 are green, a carryover from last year’s color trends, but Celery offers a different perspective.

“While deeper, earthier greens have helped create grounded, restorative spaces, we’re beginning to see that nature-inspired palette evolve in a more expressive and optimistic direction,” says Ashley Banbury, color market manager at Sherwin-Williams.

“Celery reflects this shift, bringing a lighter, more playful energy to a color family that homeowners already know and love. It shows that green can be both calming and invigorating, offering a fresh perspective on nature-inspired design while encouraging homeowners to embrace color in more personal and unexpected ways,” says Banbury.

C2’s Pueblo is one of the more dynamic colors this year, with its identity shaped by an intentional refusal to commit to a single hue.

“What makes Pueblo so fascinating is that it resists a single definition. At its heart, it’s a warm, muted rose that bridges the space between deep floral tones and earthy neutrals. Its nuanced undertones interact with the changing temperature and intensity of natural light, revealing different aspects of the color throughout the day,” says Radon.

​“That complexity brings an unusual sense of dimension to an interior. Rather than creating a static backdrop, Pueblo becomes part of the experience of living in a space.”

​In the context of this year’s color themes, Pueblo taps into the idea that creativity and movement create energy to digitally detox.

​“There’s a certain confidence in choosing a color like that. It suggests we’re ready to move beyond simply creating a sanctuary and begin using our homes as places for creativity, individuality, and renewed engagement with life,” Radon says.

​Benjamin Moore has gone all-in on timeless over trends this year with their choice of Webster Green, a classic forest green that the paint brand is betting has staying power, given how prevalent various shades of green have been in color trends over the last few years.

​Green is adaptable and inherently energizing, which makes this shade a relevant tool for homeowners who want something sturdy but stylish too. Timeless design and decor choices are becoming more important to homeowners, for the sake of affordability and sustainability too.

​“Webster Green reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected, and continually new,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, at Benjamin Moore.​

​A sultry brown with plum undertones, French Press Coffee is all about striking the right mood and elevating daily rituals, another approach to gathering energy ahead of the daily grind. It’s the color equivalent to providing time and space to savor a hot, highly flavorful cup of coffee.

​It’s a little more nuanced than some of the other moody hues released in years prior, thanks to multidimensional color that adds visual weight and interest, while broadening potential applications.

​”French Press Coffee is the kind of color that reveals itself gradually,” said Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards. “As light shifts throughout the day, its subtle plum undertone emerges, adding complexity you don’t always see in a neutral. It’s grounding and restrained yet full of character.”

Blues dominated 2023’s colors of the year for their spa-inspired calm, and Valspar is rekindling those vibes. Chosen for being familiar but fresh, Cottage Door is a mid-toned blue with warm undertones.

Sue Kim, director of color marketing at Valspar, says that the color, “is reflective and warm, with timeless appeal that feels personal and grounding. Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortlessly into the home. It creates spaces that feel balanced, comforting, and inviting.”

The color taps into consumers’ increasingly pragmatic view on home design, and the company touts it as “designed for real life.” Homeowners would rather choose a color that endures than redecorate tomorrow.

#5590. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5589. New NAR Policies Allow MLS Data-Feed Restrictions, Photo Copyright

In the face of a rapid and accelerating shift in the MLS landscape, the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) announced today that it is introducing two new optional MLS policies, focused on topics at the forefront of the ongoing debate—namely, data and membership—along with tweaks to MLS committee eligibility and a new policy statement.

According to a release from NAR, MLSs will be allowed “at their discretion” to copyright photos and property descriptions submitted by members, and restrict the use of data feeds based on criteria that are “reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants.”

“These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” said NAR CEO Nykia Wright in a statement.

The changes—approved by the Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR’s annual meetings in New Orleans—come at a time when MLSs are scrambling to keep up with demands from brokers and evolving technology. Many MLSs—both Realtor®- and broker-owned—have announced national platforms, and proactively shifted their policies around listing syndication and data.

Cameron Paine, CEO of MARIS MLS, tells RISMedia via email that “MLSs can only benefit from adoption of sensible improvements to protect their data.”

“(T)he new NAR rules are positive efforts toward that end,” he adds.

The new policy statement, also focused on data, “reinforces” that “the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and be connected to providing real estate brokerage services, preparing appraisals, or other valuations of real property.”

An NAR spokesperson clarified that MLSs can still license data for other purposes—for example, to tech companies or universities—but that this must be at the discretion of the MLS. Enforcement also remains a “local discretion” matter, the spokesperson said.

Asked if the new data feed policy could be used to restrict MLS data feeds based on broad criteria—for instance, where a participant is located geographically—the NAR spokesperson said that the use of “(l)ocal eligibility requirements will be matters of local discretion…subject to those requirements being reasonable, objective, and equally applied to all participants, and applicable laws.”

Notably, Chicago-based MRED (not affiliated with NAR) made waves in the spring by briefly cutting Zillow off from its listing feed, claiming the portal violated a different rule when it banned certain limited-marketed listings. Compass had pressured several other MLSs—unsuccessfully—to cut Zillow’s feed based on that same rule.

Compass has also been outspoken about the alleged misuse of data by MLSs, specifically by recruiting companies, and is embroiled in lawsuits with a handful of big MLSs, mostly focused on policies restricting off-MLS marketing.

The policy allowing MLSs to copyright photos and listing descriptions comes as MLSs face AI aggregation and scrapers, with at least one big MLS directly confronting AI companies that were pilfering data—including listing descriptions and photos. NAR clarified that brokers “retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content,” and can opt-out of “assigning a copyright interest to the MLS.”

“Organized real estate, including banks and lenders, depend on the MLS to provide timely, accurate and comprehensive data, but the MLS has been consistently undermined by the wholesale theft and unfettered scraping of MLS compilation data,” Paine said.

Paine also characterized the new rules as “overdue,” adding that “any efforts to improve the qualifications of those serving on the MLS Committee are welcome.”

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5586. The AI boom’s missing balance-sheet question: What has actually been verified?

GUEST COLUMN by Neil P. Osnato

I spent 13 years on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. One lesson stayed with me long after the trading jackets disappeared: A transaction could be executed, documented and perfectly valid while the assumptions that made it attractive proved less durable than anyone expected.

That distinction matters in the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. We can believe AI will transform productivity and still ask whether each financing, data-center expansion or long-term capacity agreement is supported by evidence that can survive the investment’s life.

The industry is making commitments across different clocks. Compute contracts may run for years. Debt can mature decades from now.

Servers have much shorter technology cycles. Power infrastructure, transmission upgrades and buildings may outlast several generations of the equipment they were built to support. Meanwhile, enterprise customers are still learning what they will use, how intensively they will use it and what they will pay.

None of this proves the investments are unsound. It does create a question that belongs beside revenue forecasts and capital budgets: What exactly has been verified at the moment an institution decides to rely on a promise?

An agreement to purchase compute can be commercially meaningful. It may support financing and demonstrate customer commitment. But it does not by itself establish that the underlying workloads will remain economically productive at the contracted scale, or that the customer will renew on similar terms once technology and prices change.

A serious review must separate the existence of the contract from the economic assumptions behind its duration, usage profile, counterparty capacity and renewal expectations. Contract enforceability and economic durability are related; they are not interchangeable.

A data-center campus can be announced, financed and partially constructed before all of its necessary electricity, cooling, network and equipment dependencies have become operational. A power purchase agreement is not itself proof of deliverability at the exact commissioning date. GPU orders are not proof that a facility can run the ordered cluster at the planned duty cycle.

For infrastructure planning, I use a simple sequence: requested load, evidenced load, deliverable load, energized load, utilized load and sustained demand. These are not six fancy names for the same megawatt. They describe different claims, each requiring different supporting records.

That distinction is already relevant to public grid decisions. Persistence Analytics Group has submitted comments in MISO’s Large Load Working Group proceedings on load forecasts, application and study processes, paired-resource studies and cost transparency. The recurring question is how planners preserve alignment when a proposed project’s capacity, timing or other material conditions change after an earlier study or commitment.

Financial engineering can provide meaningful protection. Minimum payments, parent guarantees, collateral requirements, termination provisions and residual-value commitments can shift or mitigate losses. They should be evaluated on their actual terms and credit strength.

But a contractual remedy is not the same as the continued usefulness of the underlying asset. A guarantee may support recovery from a counterparty while leaving the investor dependent on that counterparty’s resources, enforceability, timing and the value remaining after a disruption. Those are separate assumptions that deserve separate evidence.

This is especially important when apparently distinct exposures rely on a small set of interconnected customers, infrastructure providers, funding sources or technology assumptions. Diversifying contracts does not necessarily diversify the dependency underneath them.

Initial diligence usually asks whether a project is supportable at approval. A more durable approach asks what must remain true afterward — and which changes require the original case to be revisited before additional money is committed.

Consider a campus whose customer delays its ramp, whose power availability moves to a later year or whose equipment changes materially. Each event may be manageable on its own. But if the original financing or infrastructure decision assumed the earlier configuration, someone must decide whether the updated evidence still supports the next commitment.

That is a decision gate, not a prediction about whether AI succeeds. It calls for a documented chain: the representation being relied upon; the assumption embedded in it; the evidence supporting that assumption; the dependencies that must hold; the party bearing downside exposure; and the material change that would require reassessment.

Different specialists own different pieces. Engineers assess technical deliverability. Lawyers assess contractual rights. Accountants and finance teams assess financial statements and cash flows. Independent decision assurance asks whether those records, taken together, actually establish the proposition the capital allocator is relying on — and whether known gaps have been made explicit.

The productive-utilization debate is essential. So is the question of who will pay for AI intelligence, and at what price. But before authorizing the next investment, a chief financial officer or investment committee can ask an even more immediate question: Which assumptions are verified facts, which are binding commitments, which are conditional forecasts and which need to be revalidated because something material has changed?

A sector can produce transformational technology and disappointing returns on some of its assets. We have seen that distinction in markets before. The lesson is not to stop investing. It is to stop treating execution, delivery, utilization and durable economic value as if they were the same event.

On the trading floor, the confirmation of a trade was the beginning of understanding the position, not the end. AI infrastructure deserves the same discipline.

Neil P. Osnato is founder of Persistence Analytics Group LLC, an independent Decision Assurance™ and Infrastructure Assumption Verification™ firm. He previously spent 13 years trading on the New York Stock Exchange floor. His work focuses on the documentary evidence supporting consequential infrastructure and financial decisions. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Selected public background: MISO Large Load Working Group stakeholder feedback (LLWG-2026-7 and LLWG-2026-8), September 2026; The Bond Buyer, “Deciding About Data Centers,” October 28, 2026.

#5584. Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but will Big Tech end up winning anyway?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?

The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.

Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer.

And the AI juggernaut indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.

All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.

Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time. We can walk and chew gum at the same time if we put our mind to it. Hard to imagine the Dems could do worse than Trump and the GOP have been doing for years now.

#5583. California’s Plan To Cut Housing Red Tape Fails After Stiff Opposition From Unions and Environmentalists

Despite a wide coalition of support and millions in funding from business leaders, builders, and even some Native American tribes, California's latest effort to cut red tape around housing development failed at the polls after meeting opposition from an alliance of unions and environmental groups.

Prop 45 would have limited timelines for environmental reviews of larger projects under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA.

A landmark California state law passed in 1970, CEQA requires state and local public agencies to identify, disclose, and minimize the environmental impact of proposed building projects.

The law addresses air quality and greenhouse gas emissions, water and energy resources, habitat and wildlife preservation, noise and traffic pollution, and projects' impacts on cultural and tribal resources.

Had it passed, Prop. 45 would have limited environmental reviews on "essential" infrastructure, housing, schools, and broadband internet access projects to 365 business days and require projects to be evaluated based on the environmental standards in place when the project is applied for.

Additionally, it would have limited tribal consultation to tribes officially recognized by the federal government; 55 tribes in California have not been recognized by the federal government. It would have also required courts to rule on lawsuits related to environmental review law within 270 days and to shorten the public comment period on new projects.

“We drafted Proposition 45 with full knowledge that the road ahead wouldn't be easy, that the defenders of the broken status quo would do anything — and say anything — to protect their exclusive leverage over the permitting process for housing, clean energy, water, and public works," said Jennifer Barrera, president of the California Chamber of Commerce, which sponsored the measure. "Our diverse and vocal coalition didn't back down, working tirelessly to convince millions of California voters to take a stand against our state's affordability crisis."

That coalition included the California Building Industry Association, which donated $2.5 million, and the California Association of Realtors, which donated $1.5 million.

The PAC Building a Better California, which also mounted a successful defeat of a proposed billionaire tax, secured $10 million in donations from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

As well, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, a Southern California tribe, donated $750,000 in favor of Prop. 45.

But opponents of Prop. 45 nearly matched that amount. Schmidt's wife, philanthropist Wendy Schmidt, donated a hefty $10 million opposing the measure, but environmental groups and trade unions also gave big, creating a confounding—though not unprecedented—coalition to defeat CEQA reform.

It's not surprising that a wide coalition of environmental groups opposed Prop. 45, claiming that the measure would limit environmental review and community oversight of major building projects.

"Proposition 45 would allow many of the state’s most polluting or risky projects to go forward without meaningful consideration of health and environmental impacts, and without the community input that we all rely on," wrote Sean B. Hecht, an attorney with environmental legal defense group Earthjustice .

But environmental advocates found a somewhat unlikely ally in labor groups, who donated nearly $10 million to oppose Prop. 45.

Chris Hannan, the president of the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California told The Sacramento Bee in a statement the council opposed Prop. 45 because "it would gut longstanding protections for public and environmental review, severely limiting the ability of communities and local governments to ensure major projects are built responsibly.”

But longtime CEQA watchers say that unions oppose CEQA reform because they've often leaned on the act to settle labor disputes and negotiate favorable labor agreements.

A 2017 article by Jonathan E. Shardlow and Martin P. Stratt published in Environmental Law News argued:

"The use of CEQA litigation, or threats thereof, to leverage the execution of project labor agreements is well-known throughout the state. The process typically begins with a phone call from a law firm that regularly represents a certain union. The developer and local agency are then invited to sign a project labor agreement, and, if not interested, are informed of the union’s “environmental concerns” related to the subject project. Thereafter, CEQA litigation is often filed by the same law firm on behalf of an unincorporated association."

Earlier this year, Yes on 45 published a report finding that two law firms had made nearly $90 million filing CEQA-related lawsuits on behalf of trade unions. Yes on 45 alleged that the labor unions used the threat of the lawsuits to gain union-friendly concessions.

Labor groups have disputed this, with anti-Prop. 45 campaigner Woody Little telling The Sacramento Bee, the allegation was "desperation from a failing campaign."

That alliance between labor and environmental groups may be why nearly every governor going back to George Deukmejian, who served from 1983 to 1991, has failed to successfully reform CEQA, leading former Gov. Jerry Brown to once quip: "Reform of CEQA is the Lord's work, but unfortunately the Lord's work doesn't always get done."

Last year, Gov. Gavin Newsom was able to pass AB 130 and SB 131, which created CEQA exemptions for urban infill housing and community facilities such as health care centers and foodbanks. Those bills also provide exemptions for larger manufacturing projects that meet strict wage and labor standards.This unlikely alliance may have also led some pro-housing YIMBY groups to offer more neutral stances on Prop. 45.

In a statement about the Prop. 45, California YIMBY's policy manager Max Dubler wrote that when it comes to housing, "the central question here is how you feel about sprawl."

Generally, YIMBY groups have supported high-density development over urban sprawl, preferring to focus on urban infill housing development that promotes walkability over exurban development that is car-dependent. However even Dubler noted: "Given the scale of the housing crisis, we need all the new housing we can get. Further, lots of people want single family homes on larger lots; and they should be able to have them, to the extent that is sustainable and feasible."

Dubler went on to say that "our friends in the environmental movement have raised significant substantive concerns about this measure. Most relevant to housing voters: we should not be building new homes in the fire-prone wildland urban interface because doing so puts people in harm’s way and exacerbates our insurance crisis. The fact that Prop 45 makes it easier to build freeways but not high speed rail also gives us pause."

In 2022, California estimated it needed to build 2.5 million homes by 2030. So far, 677,000 homes have been built.

The state's housing shortage has created an affordability crisis, and is a large part of why California garnered failing grades on Realtor.com's State Affordability and Homebuilding report card.

California's median listing price is $719,000, $300,000 more than the national media listing price of $415,000. California's Legislative Analyst’s Office found that households need an income of approximately $221,000 to qualify for a mortgage on a mid-tier home — more than double the state's median income. The share of million dollar listings in the state has climbed to 30% compared with the national average of 12%.

A legislative impact report published by the state of California estimated that had Prop. 45 passed it would have cost the state up to $100 million annually, noting: "State and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges."

But once implemented, the analysis conceded that state and local governments would likely have lower project costs, though responding to environmental impacts could potentially ratchet up costs.

"In short, California has not figured out how to build enough housing. While the state's unique physical geography is a factor, state and local housing supply regulations are the driving force behind California's housing shortage," Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel previously said. "Again and again, research has shown that complex webs of local regulations and red tape – especially in California – prevent new construction, delay and shrink construction projects, and increase rents and house prices as a result," he continued.

Barrerra says the California Chamber of Commerce will continue to advocate for housing reform.

"There's simply no path forward that doesn't begin with establishing clear and consistent rules for building the essentials of a prosperous future. We will continue to advocate for reform that's both comprehensive and consequential, and we will hold elected officials accountable for whether they take action that makes a difference."

Realtor.com has reached out to the Building Industry Association of Southern California, the State Building and Construction Trades Council, Clean and Healthy California, and Building a Better California for comment.

#5582. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5581. Inside Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio—as Board Probes Co-Founder on Affair With Suspected Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under investigation by the board of the company after admitting to an intimate affair with a business executive, Alice Huang, who the U.S. government has determined to be working with Chinese intelligence.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang stated in a message to the company. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

While the board of Nvidia has claimed it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” an external counsel will be selected to investigate.

The revelation, first reported by the New York Times, is expected to have an economic impact not only on Nvidia—whose stock price has already taken a hit—but on the artificial intelligence industry as a whole, given the chipmaker’s influence.

The company was the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence bom.

According to the New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent to ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Larry Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

However, he has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan in 1963, spent his early childhood in Thailand. He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to America to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school.

While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

As the future of Nvidia's stock remains unclear, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech tycoon's expansive property portfolio.

In 2017, the tech tycoon splashed over $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is tied to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell, of Marble Management, previously told the Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Of course, Huang is also neighbors with Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech mogul owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters, which is in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.
