#5580. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

#5578. AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.

To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc,, who has some deep experience in this area.

As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.

She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.

When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family: Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.

The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:

The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AWS Supply Chain was such a useful learning experience. When Aubrey got close to the product, she saw a team working to catch up rather than lead. They had been building five modules that “largely were about getting to feature parity” with entrenched enterprise resource planning vendors that had a decades-long head start.

Connect had taken the opposite path, and it’s instructive. “They understood they weren’t going to achieve feature parity,” Aubrey said of the Connect team. Instead, they led with outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone, started narrow and built from there.

Aubrey applied that same lesson to the supply chain. She rebooted it as Connect Decisions by asking a different question: where is the pain most acute, and where is the current tooling weakest? The answer was planners. “They’re firefighting the whole time,” she said. “They’re overwhelmed by a whole bunch of signals. By the time they get to decide, the moment has passed.”

The same applies to enterprises. AI projects that stall often try to replicate an entire workflow. The ones that succeed identify a painful decision point and make it dramatically better.

Aubrey’s point about measurement deserves unpacking. “Companies are stuck on what’s the ROI of AI, and they’re looking at return on tokens and this sort of stuff,” she said. “The question is, can you move your business metrics by working in a different way?”

Her proof point is Wells Vehicle Electronics, which, according to AWS, cut inventory by 7% in three months while expanding the SKUs they actively monitor from 20 to 2,000. Nobody at Wells is talking about tokens. They’re talking about working capital. If a project can’t be tied to a metric the chief financial officer already tracks, it’s an experiment, not an investment.

Amazon started where most companies start: with software development, making AI tools available across the company. Aubrey admits there’s a bit of chaos at first. “Everyone’s just experimenting with a bunch of things,” Aubrey said.

She sees that as a feature, not a bug, because that’s where the real learning happens. “You go through this learning period of, you know what, our test coverage sucks,” she said. Fix test coverage, and you find “our pipelines suck,” so you fix pipeline health, eliminate manual intervention and deploy faster. The result in her group this year: a twofold improvement in the velocity of pushes to production.

The lesson is that the velocity didn’t come from the coding assistant. It came from fixing everything downstream that the assistant exposed. Enterprises that buy the tool and skip the plumbing will see activity rise while output stays flat.

I asked Aubrey whether Amazon has adjusted its goals to reflect what employees can now do with AI. Her answer was an honest “yes and no.” In her user experience team, roles have collapsed: designers are being pushed to ship code to an alpha environment, and Amazon has created a new “UX tech” role.

The “no” is that org design and goal-setting are still catching up. Her message to her team is blunt: “The only choice you can’t make is to own the task. You have to choose to own the outcome.” Every IT leader should borrow that line. Task-based job descriptions will age poorly.

AWS’s design philosophy for the Connect family is what she calls “humorphism,” the idea that AI should fit the way people already work, not the other way around. Her biggest concern is the lag between internal prototypes and production.

“Shipping good AI with a bad user experience will fail, in my opinion,” she said. Her team has invested heavily in closing that gap, moving beyond traditional command-based interfaces toward AI that picks up cues, remembers decisions, and carries work forward. The goal, she said, is to make AI so usable that people change how they work, not because they’re told to, but because it makes sense.

She was equally candid about maturity. TE Connectivity has scaled Connect Decisions to 2,000 planners, but Connect Talent reached general availability only in September and has early customers in deployment. Aubrey said the team is focused on getting the product right before aggressively scaling, reflecting the same “pick a wedge” discipline she applied across the Connect solutions.

What made this conversation valuable was Aubrey’s willingness to share how she thinks about building AI products that work in production, from studying what made Connect successful to applying those lessons across supply chain, hiring, health care, and customer engagement. That candor is a useful model for IT leaders, because most enterprise AI programs are stuck for the same reasons AWS’s applications once were: too much breadth, too little focus and success measured by the wrong yardstick.

The AI era won’t reward companies with the most pilots. It will reward those that pick a sharp problem, fix the plumbing it exposes, redesign work around outcomes and move the metrics they already have.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5577. Meet the Marine Veteran Flipping Historic Homes in North Carolina—and Making Sure They Qualify for VA Loans

As a North Carolina-based renovator who specializes in flipping old homes, Adam Miller knew he had a unique opportunity when the owner of the Chester House reached out to see if he could help save her historic farmhouse.

The 1886-built Davidson, NC, property was in rough shape, but Miller knew he wanted to take on the project.

“The whole house felt like a North Carolina piece of folk art,” he tells Realtor.com®. “It just felt sad to tear it down, because it was one of the oldest surviving farmhouses in Davidson.”

Citing the original beadboard walls and boxy door frames, Miller could immediately picture the property’s origin story.

“You hear about somebody building a house with their bare hands, and this is the type of house I think about, you know?” he says. “The old-school North Carolina farmer gets done for the day and he’s like, adding onto his house, or he’s just doing cool stuff because that’s what he needs to survive and live on the land. That’s the vibe I get from this house.”

Known as “Old House Adam,” Miller has been transforming historic North Carolina homes for 15 years. While he says his team can “save anything,” he’s careful with choosing projects that are also good business, avoiding properties that would be “financially irresponsible” to tackle.

“If we’re not able to make the numbers work, sometimes we have to pass on really cool, beautiful projects,” he explains.

The Chester House was a particularly exciting case for Miller and his team—which includes his wife, Jessica Miller, a talented interior designer and portrait artist.

“We actually beat out a developer that was hunting the property,” he shares, noting that this plot of land was exceptionally desirable, given its access to a 48-acre nature preserve. “It was really pretty awesome.”

They were also able to secure the two properties on either side of the Chester House, where they’ll erect “heirloom farmhouses,” leveraging vintage floor plans and salvaged materials to create something new with an old-school feel.

Although the home ended up needing much more work than initially anticipated, Miller was able to restore its original character while adding a few modern luxuries.

Two gorgeous and generously sized bathrooms were added—even if they both required extensive changes to the footprint of the home.

The kitchen underwent a more extensive renovation than he typically carries out in these kinds of projects, receiving fully-customized cabinetry. And the home’s most defining features—like the original wood floors—were given their moment to shine.

“You don’t want a house where you’ve pulled all the character out of it, but you also don’t want a house that feels like it’s still 1886,” he says.

For Miller, that means finding a balance between keeping original features and making additions that “embrace the imperfections of the house.”

In an “awkward” corner, they added “interesting bookshelves” to give the space new purpose. Built-ins and storage space were added to make the home more functional. And aesthetics were chosen to provide a mix of on-trend features and classic design, which Miller points out, are sometimes one in the same.

Miller also believes that it’s important to choose the right materials when breathing new life into an historic property.

“You’ve got to pull in a little bit of personality,” he says. “People don’t acknowledge this. It’s the material choices. If you stick to old-school materials and there’s no real plastics involved or synthetics, then you can get a lot more look for the money.”

Speaking of quality, Miller, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, is also careful to make sure his projects tick all of the boxes needed to qualify for a potential buyer to use a VA loan. He says that understanding the “code and qualifications” of a VA loan is important for renovators and builders, “Because then everybody gets to qualify and participate in home ownership.”

“I talk to a lot of veterans, and they’re like, ‘You can’t get a loan on an old house,’ and that’s 100% not true,” says Miller. “You can’t get a loan on a bad old house. But a good old house? There’s a lot of them. There’s a lot of these old houses that have survived, and they hit all the notes.”

Miller couldn’t have used a VA loan to acquire the Chester House for renovation, joking that it was in such disrepair that “VA wouldn’t have even sent somebody out to look at it originally.” But he says the loan option is a great tool, and even used one for his own home, which was built in 1906.

Now that the Chester House has been given a second chance, “even though it’s as old as it is, it would be a perfect home for a VA loan,” Miller explains.

“We replaced all the siding, there’s no chipping paint. All the windows open and operate correctly. The grading was all professionally done, so there’s no intrusion of water in the basement,” he says. “It’s got a new roof on it, the foundation doesn’t have any cracks greater than an eighth of an inch… so if you can ensure a house has all the qualifications, then you can renovate an old house and veterans can still get loans on them.”

Beyond going the extra mile to ensure a dwelling can be a great home for anyone, Miller loves to see what a renovation can do for a community.

“So many people drive by it. They’ve watched it just fall apart,” he says. “And everyone’s like, ‘Man, I wish somebody would save that thing,’ and that’s cool, too. To be the guy that people associate with watching a house fall down and all of a sudden you get to watch it be built back up.”

#5576. Significant Pent-Up Demand Could Be Released If Supply, Affordability and Confidence Improve

A wave of sidelined homebuyers could be poised to flood the housing market if a trifecta of housing supply and affordability improve and consumer confidence picks up. How likely that is remains unclear, however.

That was the theme of a market outlook delivered this past Friday by National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun at the Residential Economic Issues and Trends Forum at NAR NXT in New Orleans.

According to a release, Yun compared today’s economy with the year 2000, noting since then, the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million, and payroll jobs have risen from 132 million to 159 million. He said housing wealth has grown from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are running near 4 million this year, below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000.

“Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said.

On supply, Yun noted that inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September.

“Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.”

Yun said a rebound in consumer confidence would also be key. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the economy has added jobs, he said.

“If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said.

Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented highlights from the newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the historic low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40.

“First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They’re also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.”

Sellers stayed in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest on record.

“The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” said Lautz. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.”

Use of real estate professionals remained strong: 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent.

“Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said.

#5573. Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa.

Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs.

Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. The company plans to release the model’s weights under an open-source license next week.

#5572. Minnesota Remodeler Is Banned for Life After Demolishing Rooms and Skipping Out

A Minnesota contractor promised homeowners he could transform their properties with extensive renovations. Instead, many say they were left with unfinished work, empty bank accounts and little to show for the tens of thousands of dollars they had handed over.

Now, Ryan David Pietron, and his company, Affordable Home Remodeling, LLC., have been permanently banned from Minnesota's residential construction industry and ordered to pay more than $1 million after a state investigation found they had defrauded dozens of homeowners out of a combined $518,000, according to the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.

"Pietron would perform token demolition work, or none at all, before disappearing with his customers’ money," the AG's office said in a statement.

On Nov. 5, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announced a judgment against Pietron and the company, requiring them to pay $518,000 in restitution to victims, another $518,000 in civil penalties to the state and $33,000 to cover the attorney general's costs and legal fees.

“Pietron played fast and loose with people’s home renovation dreams and needs,” Ellison said. “He counted on people giving up and moving on. Instead, Minnesotans reported this scheme to my office, and now he’s permanently out of this business and will pay for his fraud.”

In a separate criminal case brought by Wright County Attorney’s Office, Pietron pleaded guilty on Nov. 3 to felony theft in connection with some of the same conduct that was the subject of the AG’s civil investigation.

The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office sued Pietron and Affordable Home Remodeling in October 2025 on behalf of Minnesota homeowners who were left with unfinished renovations and losses totaling thousands of dollars.

Pietron was never licensed as a residential building contractor and was banned by the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry from claiming to be a licensed contractor—but told customers he was licensed anyway, according to the attorney general’s office.

In an attempt to squeeze more money out of homeowners, investigators say Pietron issued fake progress updates and forged phony invoices.

In one case, a homeowner had hired Pietron to complete work on her kitchen in October of 2024. Nearly a year later, the homeowner was out of town and contacted Pietron to find out the status of the work.

Pietron told her that a crew was currently working on the home. But when the homeowner checked the home’s security cameras, they discovered no one had arrived at the property.

Pietron gave other excuses for the delay including that several trucks had broken down. He then disappeared from the job completely and took the homeowner’s money with him, according to the complaint.

In another case, a customer who had hired Affordable Home Remodeling waited several months for work to begin on his home, only to be given an invoice for supplies which had allegedly been ordered on the homeowner’s behalf.

But when the homeowner contacted the supplier listed on the invoice, they had no record of such items having been ordered by Affordable Home Remodeling. Pietron allegedly made off with $30,000 for work on that property that had never started.

Some of the homeowners managed to track him down and when they did, he had promised to issue them refunds but failed to do so.

Investigators identified more than 50 Minnesota homeowners who lost a combined $518,000.

The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office is urging homeowners to research contractors and companies before signing agreements, request important information in writing and carefully review contracts and other documents.

While hiring a licensed contractor does not guarantee a successful home improvement project, there are many protections for consumers who hire licensed contractors.

Licensed contractors are required to carry liability insurance and property damage insurance. Consumers can also use a free license lookup tool maintained by the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry to verify whether a contractor is properly licensed.

Eligible consumers who obtain a judgment against a licensed contractor for fraudulent or dishonest conduct can recover up to $75,000 from the Contractor Recovery Fund if they are unable to collect the judgment from the contractor.

#5571. For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.

Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier.

Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard.

Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data.

A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers.

The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers.

Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers.

The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month.

Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas, where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale.

While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.”

The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market.

The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer’s market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes

The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months.

House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas.

But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s  market may offer an opportunity.

“Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova, a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said.

Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova.

For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said.

Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs.

Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier.

The typical condo that sold in September spent 63 days on the market before going under contract, up from 35 days five years earlier.

Condo buyers in Texas had more negotiating powers than anywhere else in the country in September. San Antonio had the widest seller-buyer gap among the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas, with an estimated 459% more sellers than buyers. Houston followed with 322% more sellers than buyers, then came Austin, with 258% more.

Miami also had one of the nation’s widest gaps, with an estimated 274% more condo sellers than buyers in September, ranking third.

“San Antonio condos may have an attractive purchase price, but buyers are looking at the total monthly payment. Because we have so many affordable single-family homes available, many buyers choose a house when the payments are close,” said Derrell Skillman, a Redfin Premier agent in San Antonio, TX.

Skillman added San Antonio has a large military community, and its housing market tends to follow the military’s permanent change-of-station (PCS) season.

“We usually see more military-related activity during the spring and summer when families are transferring in and out of the area. Once that period slows down, the drop in demand can be more noticeable, especially in a smaller segment like condos,” he said. “HOA costs, financing restrictions, builder incentives, softer investor demand and the slowdown after the military PCS season are all contributing to the buyer’s market for condos,” said Skillman.

Meanwhile, new construction is adding to the softness in Sun Belt markets. The Sun Belt is home to nine of the 10 metros where condo sellers outnumber buyers most.

Nassau County, NY, was the only metro area among the 50 analyzed that was a seller’s market for condos in September. There were 32% fewer sellers than buyers, with an estimated 1,545 buyers compared with 1,052 sellers.

“Condo buyers are mostly people who want maintenance-free living,” said William Ortiz, a Redfin Premier agent in Long Island, NY. “They want to have an easier lifestyle as opposed to all the maintenance and upkeep that comes with a house. Common charges are expensive, but they’re willing to pay for that convenience.”

According to Sandra Glaser, a Redfin senior agent in Long Island, condo demand is coming from three main groups: first-time buyers priced out of single-family homes, particularly those moving from the city to the suburbs; downsizers seeking less upkeep; and investors looking for rental income from properties that require minimal maintenance.

Five other metros — Chicago, Milwaukee, New Brunswick, Newark and San Francisco — had balanced condo markets, where the difference between buyers and sellers was within 10%.

San Francisco’s condo market, for example, is heating up, with the median sale price jumping 20% year over year to nearly $1.2 million in September. Khan, the Redfin senior economist, ties the area’s renewed housing demand to the AI boom, which is attracting highly paid workers and fueling homebuying.

As a senior data reporter, Dian uses data and quantitative analysis to tell stories about economy and real estate. She also builds databases and creates statistical charts that visualize data trends. Previously, Dian spent seven years as a senior data reporter at USA TODAY.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5570. Court Report: Tuccori Settlements on Hold as Judge Requests Further Logistics

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

Tuccori settlement on hold after judge request

The approval of settlement agreements with more than 20 real estate companies in a major antitrust lawsuit filed by recent homebuyers challenging commission practices in the residential real estate market has been put on hold by a judge following a request for more information.

The settlements in the Tuccori v. At World Properties commission lawsuit were preliminarily approved back in May, but final approval has been put on hold as Judge Lindsay C. Jenkins has put in a request for additional information on five topics.

Firstly, Jenkins asked for clarification on a concern that was previously raised at a hearing: The valuation of claims filed, namely that “resolving 1/8 of all claims for 1/8 of what you paid to resolve the other 7/8 of all claims does not imply you valued the 1/8 and 7/8 equally on a per claim basis.”

Other requests include how each settler’s “ability to pay and transaction volume influenced their proposed settlement,” further information for the court to be able to arrive at the “net expected value of continued litigation,” benchmarks for “substantive adequacy from other indirect purchaser class actions,” and lastly, an estimation of per claimant and per class member recovery.

The National Association of Realtors®, one of the settlers in the case, said in a statement that it “continues to believe the Tuccori settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the class.”

“The settlement offers meaningful protections across the industry, providing a broad release for REALTOR® members, REALTOR® associations, MLSs, and those brokerages that meet the settlement’s eligibility requirements,” the statement read. “NAR remains committed to fostering fair, transparent, and pro-consumer real estate markets while providing resources and value to our REALTOR® members nationwide.”

NAR added that the judge’s request is “a routine part of the class action settlement approval process, consistent with the judge’s role in evaluating the fairness of the settlement.”

“NAR is committed to abiding by the judge’s request to provide the Court with information in a timely and efficient manner, including working with the other parties, to demonstrate the settlement is fair and reasonable,” the statement concluded.

Briefs on the topics are due by Dec. 14, after which time the court will say if it needs further responses.

Fair housing lawsuit against Bank of America dismissed

A racial-discrimination lawsuit filed against Bank of America and a Virginia-based appraiser has been dismissed.

The suit was filed by Darchelle Braxton, a Black woman who last summer attempted to secure a loan for home improvements on an investment property. She claimed in her filing that an initial appraisal ordered by Bank of America valued her property at $135,000, but a subsequent second appraisal valued it more than 50% higher, at $208,000.

The appraiser—Velox Valuations—filed a motion to dismiss, refuting Braxton’s claims that it provided a “shockingly low” valuation on her property due to alleged “material errors, omissions, and inconsistencies,” which stemmed from racial bias. Such errors included allegedly using an incorrect map reference, using an incorrect neighborhood valuation, only using two comparable properties, inconsistent descriptions of the property’s condition, and more.

The suit was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

With the many legal battles the portal has faced as of late, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business” during its Q3 2026 earnings call.

CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann added that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

The portal is currently still facing a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5569. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data

In A Nutshell:  Mortgage rates are coming down as investors dial back expectations for rate hikes. But that could change: Key inflation data comes out this week.

Two highlights from a busy election week:

This week’s economics highlight is the CPI inflation data coming Tuesday, coupled with Friday’s PPI data. Together, the two will form a complete picture of the core PCE inflation measure the Fed uses. The consensus forecast has core CPI coming in at 0.2% month-over-month, down slightly from last month. Forecasters are expecting a small statistical distortion in the data due to last year’s government shutdown. A very low read for inflation might convince the Fed to hold off on hiking rates at the December meeting, but they could just as easily write it off as one data point. They would evaluate how broader financial conditions have changed since the last meeting, including any further improvement in rates.

Many Fed officials are holding speaking engagements this week. The ones to watch are Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on Tuesday; Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Monday, Tuesday, and Friday; Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday; and New York Fed President John Williams on Thursday.

#5568. OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation

OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as sources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today.

The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.

It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.

Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal, one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.

The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well.

The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing.

In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending.

Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving.

#5567. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5565. EXCLUSIVE: Former NFL Star Chris Simms Sells 300-Year-Old Greenwich Home For $5.5 Million

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has sold his historic Connecticut estate for $5.5 million—after reducing the initial $8 million asking price several times.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately led to Simms landing a buyer for the dwelling, Realtor.com® can exclusively reveal. The property has closed for $5.5 million.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor plan that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now moving to a new state and want to pass their current dwelling to a new owner who will treasure it as much as they have.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

Simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the New England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

#5564. AI cyber resilience and the trust gap

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante and Krista Case

Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets.

In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake?

Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit.

Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes.

Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments.

We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions:

These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require.

Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI.

Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested.

These findings come from a small sample of in-depth interviews conducted with our partner Qualitate. The conversations allowed us to explore what customers have tested, the additional security work their own AI creates and what it takes to resume a business process safely. One healthcare practitioner phrased the disconnect between confidence and readiness as follows:

No, we have not completed any tabletop exercises as it pertains to an AI agent or other similar attacks. We’re highly confident because these are scenarios similar to non-AI incidents we have handled before.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Across the interviews, respondents who did express confidence often drew heavily on existing ransomware and incident response playbooks. Their experience with non-AI incidents understandably provides a degree of trust. But it also raises a concern in that organizations may assume that an agent taking an incorrect action can be handled in the same way as an insider or external attacker doing something similar. We don’t believe existing playbooks cover all scenarios.

Rather, we believe that assumption needs to be tested against the specific demands of an agent incident. The interviews revealed a mixed picture of true validation:

Complete business recovery requires an organization to reconstruct a sequence of authorized actions, identify incorrect outcomes, repair downstream effects and safely resume the affected business process. Demonstrating that the full sequence works is a nontrivial exercise.

The speed, scale and interconnected nature of agent activity makes that even more challenging. Actions can affect multiple systems and processes, creating consequences that existing playbooks need to account for. We see a risk of false confidence when organizations assume that their experience with traditional non-AI incidents will translate automatically. Testing needs to establish how well their capabilities hold up under the conditions an agent can create, which may be novel.

Bottom line: Evidence of validated, end-to-end business recovery from an agent incident remains limited in our study. We believe organizations should exercise their existing playbooks against realistic agent scenarios, with safe business resumption as the measure of success.

Our interviews raised questions about tooling, maturity and the processes needed to prove that existing capabilities work for agentic AI. Two findings as shown below highlight the limited reach of detection and reconstruction capabilities in the organizations studied:

One healthcare practitioner’s assessment of the controls already implemented underscores the trust gap:

No, for the ones that have been implemented, we have not tested or validated that they work.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Enterprises already have identity systems, application logs, data protection tools and the like, along with established incident response processes. They are trying to extend these capabilities to AI. The central challenge is validating that the tools can reconstruct activity across an entire agent workflow.

Agents interact with multiple applications, invoke tools and autonomously trigger downstream actions. Each system may capture its own events without providing a coherent record of the complete workflow. Incident response requires correlating those records to establish which agent acted and under what authority, then tracing the tools it invoked and the changes that resulted.

This reminds us of the early days of disaster recovery, when organizations would test failover but hesitate to test failback because they were nervous about what might happen. We see a similar reluctance to ask questions that could expose gaps in readiness or cause downstream problems. The concern is whether the connected tools and processes will hold up under realistic agent incident conditions.

Bottom line: Organizations need to exercise the full agent workflow under realistic conditions, including a plausible worst-case event, and validate that their tools and processes can reconstruct the activity and support the response.

Our assessment of the field interviews highlights both the technical and business dimensions involved in a recovery. An AI agent can use legitimate access to change a record incorrectly or send a message that should never have been sent. A backup may work and the restored systems may appear healthy while the business remains unable to resume safely.

StorageTek veteran Fred Moore, an early mentor to Dave Vellante, coined the phrase: “Backup is one thing, recovery is everything.” The scope of recovery continues to expand as organizations consider the consequences of agents acting across business systems.

A director of information security at a media and entertainment firm described the problem this way:

We could restore our systems, we could restore within our recovery objectives, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that it’s safe. The bottleneck here would be trust.

— Director of information security, media and entertainment

Recovery point objectives or RPO and recovery time objectives or RTO are the so-called business metrics. But business users need more meaningful key performance indicators that resonate — specifically, what a trusted, viable service looks like and how that condition can be verified. That includes establishing who needs to participate in recovery and who signs off that operations can safely resume.

This direction needs to come from the top down; and be verified bottom up. Business leaders must define the requirements, with IT and security acting as partners to provide the underlying technology and help achieve the required outcome. The responsibility extends beyond the traditional data protection team’s work of recovering data and systems.

Incorrect transactions, human error and failures that ripple across systems have existed for a long time. Agentic AI adds two complications:

That requires a comprehensive view of what went wrong and what needs to happen to recover. The organization must be able to trace the agent’s activity and evaluate the resulting business state against clear criteria for safe operation.

Bottom line: Recovery requires explicit criteria for verifying that a business service can be trusted and clear responsibility for approving its return to operation. The business must set that direction, with IT and security providing the capabilities to carry it out.

Humans in the loop help organizations restrict what agents can do. Resilience also has to account for what happens when a human misses an incorrect action or cannot keep pace with agents operating at machine speed. Two statements from the same CIO illustrates the issue:

So the given scenario will be detected by human beings before the AI agents can take the actions.

If it really happens, currently we do not have the capability to roll back the agent’s action.

— Chief information officer, real estate and construction

The first statement shows confidence that human oversight will catch the problem. The second acknowledges a missing “undo command” if the human oversight fails. This captures why approvals and recovery testing need to advance together. Reliance on human intervention can bring a false sense of security and defer attention to the recovery details needed when a mistake gets through.

Our field study also revealed how customers are weighing the tradeoffs around autonomy, with organizations generally still containing what their agents can do. Those decisions become particularly important when agents receive authority to take remedial actions during an incident or recovery.

The level of autonomy granted should reflect the risk of the action. Before allowing an agent to approve or execute a remedial action, organizations need to understand the consequences of an incorrect decision. That calls for a tiered approach built around two considerations:

We expect human approval to become an increasingly significant bottleneck over the next six to 12 months. Organizations need to establish these boundaries as they begin trusting agents to take more remedial actions.

Bottom line: Human oversight and recovery testing need to develop together. As organizations delegate more authority to agents, they must account for mistakes, the limits of human review and the risk associated with each action.

A retail practitioner described a viable approach to rehearsing an agent incident and we see this as a best practice. Specifically, this firm replays the agent’s actions in a replica environment, investigating the root cause and using granular snapshots to understand the transactional effects. The respondent explicitly confirmed that the approach had been tested in the sandbox with the following statement:

Yes, if the agent went across multiple systems, my approach is to replay this within my sandbox environment, which is a full replica of all of the systems.

— Director of information technology, retail

The value of this approach is in reproducing the sequence of events and investigating their effects across systems. Our assessment of what such an exercise should confirm is anchored on three outcomes:

We see these as minimum viable expectations for the evidence an exercise should produce.

We use the term digital twin here as a broad analogy for this approach. A fuller digital twin would involve a richer representation of business processes, dependencies and state. We believe the industry still has work to do in that direction, and that work will become more important as enterprises use AI to run critical functions. In addition, it will further expand the notion of recovery as the state of the business will become increasingly more complicated as agents perform more of the work.

The respondent also acknowledged a limitation saying: larger transaction volumes could require more time for reconciliation. Replaying actions and identifying affected transactions provides useful information, while the time needed to resolve their consequences remains an open item. Richer simulations of business environments could help organizations test agent behavior and prepare for what a failure might look like in production.

In other words, testing the recovery sequence in a variety of scenarios inside a digital twin of the business prior to pushing the process into production. Further, this “red teaming” exercise must be ongoing – expanding the concept of continuous data protection into the state of a firm’s operations in more granular snapshots.

Bottom line: This example offers a practical approach to reproducing agent actions, investigating their consequences and rehearsing recovery. Its value also points toward the need for richer representations of the business processes those agents affect.

If a chief information security officer takes one action from this study, we recommend exercising an agent incident affecting one consequential workflow already in production. Choose a workflow in which an agent has permission to act across multiple systems, and design the exercise to include incorrect actions taken with valid credentials and permissions.

The exercise should also include a scenario requiring human approval. This helps establish the boundaries around where autonomy is appropriate and where human oversight remains necessary.

Validation by the business owner is essential. Security teams can establish that an incident has been contained and provide evidence of what happened. The business owner must determine whether the resulting business state is acceptable. That decision needs to account for the consequences of the agent’s actions and any remediation work still required.

The exercise should document what was proved, what remains untested and which teams are responsible for closing the remaining gaps. That evidence should also inform decisions about how much authority an agent receives. The organization needs to understand its ability to reverse or correct actions and recover their consequences as it considers granting greater autonomy.

The discussions at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit reinforced the themes emerging from the field study. Conversations with vendors, practitioners and researchers underscored the need to build resilience and recovery into agent deployments from the outset. Evidence that these capabilities work becomes essential as agentic workloads move into production.

The challenge includes preserving and recovering a trusted business state when an agent produces an incorrect outcome despite having legitimate credentials. Organizations need to understand how those outcomes affect their operations and what it will take to address them.

Existing investments in data protection infrastructure, security and recovery remain critical. The work ahead is to identify the gaps that emerge under the new requirements and pressures created by enterprise AI. That requires collaboration across internal teams and with vendors to understand where capabilities need to improve.

Bottom line: We believe trust in enterprise AI requires tested evidence that organizations can understand what agents have done, stop them, reconstruct their actions and recover to a healthy business state. Our research indicates that organizations still have work to do to demonstrate that their existing security and recovery capabilities can meet that requirement.

#5563. Why Now Is the Time to Prepare Senior Homes for the Spring Market

For seniors preparing to sell a home they’ve lived in for decades, fall may be the ideal time to start downsizing before spring brings a new wave of buyers. When the weather starts to cool and the leaves start to fall from the trees, it can feel like a natural time to reset, to refresh a living space and prepare for the next life chapter.

As families shift holiday decorations, reorganize storage and prepare for the end of the year, it can also be a natural opportunity to begin sorting through a lifetime of furniture, keepsakes and belongings before a home goes on the market.

Nan Hayes, VP of Business Development at Caring Transitions, a company specializing in transforming the way seniors and their families transition through life’s stages, talks about the various aspects of preparing now for homeselling later.

Why is fall a good time to begin downsizing before a spring sale?

Fall can be a good time to adjust old habits and set new goals. As the season changes, it creates a natural opportunity to take stock of our homes and begin letting go of things we no longer need.

For homeowners considering a spring home sale, fall is a good time to begin downsizing and decluttering. Starting months before listing provides time to address repairs, sort through belongings and make decisions without the added pressure of an active home sale. As a bonus, a more organized home can also make holiday entertaining easier.

Homeowners can choose to sort, donate, sell, gift or dispose of excess belongings themselves, or bring in professionals to handle some of the more time-consuming tasks. Either way, starting early can help ensure the home is ready when it is time to list.

For real estate agents, the journey from lead to listing can take several months. Timelines become longer when homeowners are waiting for more favorable market conditions, completing home preparations or waiting on another life event, such as end of the school year, or the birth of a child.

For older adults who are downsizing into a senior living community or other care setting, the process may take even longer. Selling a family home in later life can be a major task. Many times, the home holds a lot of memories as well as a lot of ‘stuff.’ Beginning early gives families time to plan the transition and make thoughtful decisions along the way.

How can decades of belongings affect a home’s perceived space?

Even a spacious home can feel smaller when closets, cabinets, garages and rooms are filled with belongings.

Reducing excess items before listing helps buyers focus on the home rather than its contents. With fewer distractions, buyers can better understand the storage space, room sizes and possibilities the property offers.

Removing excess belongings and highly personal items can also help buyers imagine themselves living in the home. The space feels more open, and the features of the property become easier to see.

Why can waiting until a home is listed create unnecessary delays?

Once a home is listed, the clock starts ticking. If the home is not yet market-ready, the remaining tasks make the home less appealing than others on the market, and can interfere with showings, or complicate the sale and closing process.

Rushing through all the tasks at the very end isn’t a good solution either. If sorting, organizing, packing, donating, selling belongings, repairing the home, and moving all have to happen at once, the home seller can quickly become overwhelmed, and they may stop the entire process.

Starting early separates the emotional work of downsizing from the time-sensitive work of selling.

How can agents approach emotionally difficult downsizing conversations?

When clients are overwhelmed by years of possessions, unsure where to begin, or suffering from decision fatigue, they need a clear plan and calm communication that stems from a place of empathy rather than urgency.

Instead of saying: “You really need to get rid of all this!” Try: “You don’t have to figure this out all at once. Let’s start with what you would like to take with you, and then we’ll come up with a plan for everything else.”

This shifts the conversation away from what the client feels they have to give up or get rid of, so they can instead focus on what comes next. For many homeowners, belongings represent decades of memories, family milestones, and important moments. Recognizing that emotional connection can make difficult conversations easier and help clients feel supported rather than rushed.

Agents do not have to solve every part of the transition themselves. They can provide direction, connect clients with reliable relocation resources, and help break a large project into manageable steps.

How can families use the holidays to start sorting, organizing, and letting go?

The holidays may provide a natural opportunity to start on home projects because families are already spending time together. Rather than turning every family gathering into a major downsizing event, use the time to share memories, make a few decisions, and start conversations about the future.

Families might look through photographs, collections or keepsakes together. Consider digitizing large collections so they can be shared with family members. Share the stories behind meaningful belongings or write those stories down.

Invite children and grandchildren to choose items that are meaningful to them. Tackle one closet, cabinet, collection, or small area together. Identify which belongings might be donated, gifted, sold, or included in an estate sale or online auction.

Contact professional downsizing, relocation, estate sale, and auction resources early to request estimates and reserve time before spring schedules begin to fill. The goal is not to spend the holidays cleaning out the house or emptying every room. It is simply to start a conversation, make a plan, complete a few manageable tasks that can help build momentum. In short, a little progress now can mean fewer decisions and less pressure when it is time to list the home.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

Routine maintenance, sensible storage, suitable flood protection and a clear emergency plan can help homeowners prepare more effectively. The right approach depends on the property, its surroundings and the conditions it may face. Read more.
